# Symmetric matrices, the spectral theorem and quadratic forms

You are blindfolded on a landscape. You may choose a direction, take a step, and measure the height. Can you discover the landscape's principal axes without seeing it? Can two directions both point uphill while a direction between them points downhill? Can a perfectly flat reading conceal a saddle?

For a quadratic landscape, those questions have exact answers. A symmetric matrix is the instruction sheet; its eigenvectors are the axes; its eigenvalues tell you what happens along each axis. We will build that dictionary, prove why it works, and learn when a numerical test has said less than it appears to.

## 0. Where this is going

Four results carry this chapter: real symmetric matrices have orthonormal eigenbases; Rayleigh quotients reveal eigenvalues through constrained extrema; eigenvalue signs classify quadratic forms; and positive definiteness is equivalent to a Cholesky factorization with positive diagonal.

All matrices and vectors here are real, and orthogonality means the standard Euclidean dot product. Matrices are square unless stated otherwise. Write eigenvalues in **ascending** order, λ₁≤⋯≤λₙ, including repetitions. A symmetric matrix satisfies Aᵀ=A; an orthogonal matrix satisfies QᵀQ=I. These are different properties.

Study sections 1–8 with pencil and the linked experiment. Section 9 supplies three runnable stdlib Python tasks. The local NumPy and PyTorch exercises are experiments, not prerequisites for the proofs. The 28 hours include reconstructing arguments, implementing algorithms, and attempting the checkpoint. We use one explicitly named fact from analysis: a continuous function attains a maximum on the unit sphere. The spectral proof needs no differentiation. The final curvature application previews calculus without using it to prove the linear algebra.

## 1. Symmetry means reciprocal measurements

Aᵀ=A is more than a mirror pattern in a table. It says

$$
u^{\mathsf T}Av=(Au)^{\mathsf T}v\qquad\text{for all }u,v.
$$

The component of Av along u equals the component of Au along v. Choosing coordinate vectors recovers aᵢⱼ=aⱼᵢ, so the measurement rule and the entry rule are equivalent.

This reciprocity repairs a failure from Module 6. If S is invariant under a symmetric A, then its orthogonal complement is also invariant. Indeed, for x∈S⊥ and s∈S,

$$
s^{\mathsf T}Ax=(As)^{\mathsf T}x=0,
$$

because As∈S. There is no traffic between these perpendicular rooms in either direction. A nonsymmetric shear preserves the horizontal line but can send the vertical line into it.

If Au=λu and Av=μv, reciprocity gives (λ−μ)uᵀv=0. **Distinct eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix have orthogonal eigenspaces.** Repeated eigenvalues need care: for A=I, both (1,0) and (1,1) are eigenvectors, and they are not orthogonal. The claim is that an orthonormal eigenbasis can be *chosen*, not that arbitrary returned eigenvectors are already perpendicular.

We still owe existence: perpendicularity of eigenvectors does not itself produce even one eigenvector. That is the next section's work.

> **Practice — Foundation:** For A=[[2,1],[1,3]], compare e₁ᵀAe₂ with (Ae₁)ᵀe₂.
>
> **Hint:** Each expression reads one off-diagonal entry. Then identify which equality would fail if only a₁₂ changed.
>
> **Practice — Core:** For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\) and its eigenvector q=(1,1), check that A(1,−1) is perpendicular to q. Then prove for any symmetric A with Aq=λq that q⊥ is invariant, without assuming an eigenbasis.
>
> **Hint:** A(1,−1)=(1,−1). For general x⊥q, move A across the dot product: qᵀ(Ax)=(Aq)ᵀx=λqᵀx=0.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** For \(A=\operatorname{diag}(3,3,5)\), give two nonorthogonal eigenvectors, and explain why they do not contradict the claim that a symmetric matrix's eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal.
>
> **Hint:** Every nonzero vector in span(e₁,e₂) is an eigenvector for 3, for example (1,0,0) and (1,1,0). Their eigenvalues coincide, while any eigenvector for 5 is still orthogonal to both.

## 2. Find one axis, then reduce the room

Define the **quadratic form** \(q_A(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Ax\). Its restriction to unit vectors is a directional measurement, unaffected by how long the test arrow originally was.

**Theorem 23 — the real spectral theorem.** For every real symmetric n×n matrix A, there is a real orthogonal Q and a real diagonal Λ such that

$$
A=Q\Lambda Q^{\mathsf T}.
$$

Conversely, any matrix with such a factorization is symmetric.

*Proof, first find an axis.* The continuous function xᵀAx attains its maximum λ on the unit sphere; let q be a maximizing unit vector. For any unit v⊥q and any real t, the vector (q+tv)/√(1+t²) is unit. Maximality and symmetry give

$$
\frac{\lambda+2t\,v^{\mathsf T}Aq+t^2v^{\mathsf T}Av}{1+t^2}\le\lambda,
\qquad
2t\,v^{\mathsf T}Aq+t^2(v^{\mathsf T}Av-\lambda)\le0.
$$

If vᵀAq were nonzero, choose the sign of a sufficiently small t to make the linear term positive and larger than the quadratic term in magnitude. Contradiction. Thus Aq is perpendicular to every v⊥q, so Aq lies on q's line. Its component along q is qᵀAq=λ; hence Aq=λq.

*Then reduce.* Section 1 shows q⊥ is invariant. In any orthonormal basis of that (n−1)-dimensional space, the restricted matrix is again symmetric. Apply the same argument inductively, with dimension one as the base case. Joining those eigenvectors to q gives an orthonormal basis. Its column equations say AQ=QΛ, and Q⁻¹=Qᵀ gives the factorization. For the converse, transpose QΛQᵀ and use Λᵀ=Λ.

This proof produces real eigenvalues and enough eigenvectors together. It does not first assume distinct roots, compute a characteristic polynomial, or claim an arbitrary real matrix has a real eigenvector.

**A worked change of coordinates.** Let

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},\quad
q_1=\frac{(1,-1)}{\sqrt2},\quad q_2=\frac{(1,1)}{\sqrt2}.
$$

Direct multiplication gives eigenvalues 1 and 3. With Q=[q₁ q₂], the coordinates y=Qᵀx satisfy

$$
x^{\mathsf T}Ax=y_1^2+3y_2^2,\qquad \|x\|^2=y_1^2+y_2^2.
$$

Reading eigen-coordinates and taking dot products are now the same operation. Unlike a general eigenbasis, this change of coordinates preserves lengths and angles. It may include a reflection; “orthogonal” does not mean “rotation only.”

> **Practice — Foundation:** For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\), \(q_1=(1,-1)/\sqrt2\), and \(q_2=(1,1)/\sqrt2\), verify Aq₁=q₁ and Aq₂=3q₂.
>
> **Hint:** Multiply before dividing by √2. The normalization affects length, not the eigenvalue equation.
>
> **Practice — Core:** In the maximality inequality \(2t\,v^{\mathsf T}Aq+t^2(v^{\mathsf T}Av-\lambda)\le0\), suppose \(v^{\mathsf T}Aq=-0.5\) and \(v^{\mathsf T}Av-\lambda=-1\). Evaluate the left side at t=0.1 and t=−0.1. Which sign exposes the contradiction, and why must the argument permit both signs of t?
>
> **Hint:** The left side is \(-t-t^2\). Only t<0 makes the linear term positive, and for small |t| the quadratic term cannot cancel it.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Prove the converse of the spectral theorem and use it to rule out an orthogonal diagonalization of [[1,1],[0,1]].
>
> **Hint:** Transpose the proposed factorization. The triangular shear is not symmetric, even though its only eigenvalue is real.

## 3. The Rayleigh quotient is a weighted vote

For x≠0 define

$$
R_A(x)=\frac{x^{\mathsf T}Ax}{x^{\mathsf T}x}.
$$

It measures quadratic value per squared unit of length. R_A(cx)=R_A(x) for every nonzero real c. In eigen-coordinates y=Qᵀx,

$$
R_A(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i w_i,\qquad
w_i=\frac{y_i^2}{\sum_j y_j^2},\qquad w_i\ge0,\quad\sum_iw_i=1.
$$

The signs of y disappear; the squared fractions of length are the votes. This is why a Rayleigh reading can lie between eigenvalues without itself being an eigenvalue.

**Theorem 24 — variational characterization.** For symmetric A,

$$
\min_{x\ne0}R_A(x)=\lambda_1,\qquad
\max_{x\ne0}R_A(x)=\lambda_n.
$$

Equality at either extreme holds exactly when x lies in the corresponding extreme eigenspace. More generally,

$$
\lambda_k=\min_{\dim S=k}\ \max_{0\ne x\in S}R_A(x).
$$

*Proof.* The weighted-average formula proves the bounds and equality cases. For the second statement, any k-dimensional S intersects T=span(q_k,…,q_n) nontrivially: dim S+dim T=n+1, so a trivial intersection would exceed the ambient dimension. A nonzero x in this intersection has R_A(x)≥λ_k. Therefore the maximum over S is at least λ_k. Choosing S=span(q₁,…,q_k) attains that bound. Maxima on each subspace's unit sphere exist by the same compactness fact used earlier.

There is also a practical ladder: minimize R_A subject to being perpendicular to previously chosen q₁,…,qₖ₋₁. The next minimum is λₖ. For repeated eigenvalues, the particular orthonormal axes inside that eigenspace remain a choice.

**One measurement, two interpretations.** For unit x, R=xᵀAx is the projection coefficient of Ax onto x. Write r=Ax−Rx. Then

$$
x^{\mathsf T}r=0,\qquad
\|r\|^2=\sum_i w_i(\lambda_i-R)^2.
$$

The residual measures the spread of the eigenvalues receiving votes. Consequently at least one λᵢ satisfies |λᵢ−R|≤‖r‖. This eigenvalue proximity guarantee uses symmetry. A small residual still does not identify *which* eigenvalue or certify that a direction is close to one uniquely chosen eigenvector when eigenvalues cluster.

**Predict before calculating.** For diag(−1,1) and x=(1,1)/√2, R=0. Is x a zero eigenvector?

<details><summary>Reveal the measurement's missing information</summary>

No. Ax=(−1,1)/√2 is perpendicular to x, so the projection coefficient vanishes, but the residual has length 1. The weighted votes cancel. A zero quadratic value is not generally a zero image.

</details>

> **Practice — Foundation:** Compute R for diag(1,3) at x=(1,2), and state its two bounds.
>
> **Hint:** The eigenvalue weights are 1/5 and 4/5, not 1/3 and 2/3. Divide by squared length.
>
> **Practice — Core:** For A=diag(1,3) and unit x=(1,2)/√5, compute R, the residual r=Ax−Rx, and ‖r‖². Then prove \(\|r\|^2=\sum_i(\lambda_i-R)^2y_i^2\) by expressing Ax and Rx in the same orthonormal eigenbasis.
>
> **Hint:** Here R=13/5 and r=(−8,4)/(5√5), so ‖r‖²=0.64. In general the coefficient of r along q_i is (λ_i−R)y_i, and Pythagoras turns its norm squared into a sum.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** For diag(1,4,9), explain why every two-dimensional subspace contains a vector with Rayleigh quotient at least 4.
>
> **Hint:** Intersect it with span(e₂,e₃). Count dimensions before trying to guess a direction.

## 4. A landscape with three linked views

The laboratory builds A=Q diag(λ₁,λ₂)Qᵀ from two eigenvalue controls and an axis angle. Here subscripts name the **controlled axes**, so the two values need not stay sorted. Move the probe around the unit circle to read R; move the eigenvalues through zero to change the landscape. Sliders are keyboard accessible, and you can drag the probe directly. The second plot traces every directional reading; the dot on that curve is the same probe as in the first plot.

```lab
la-quadform
```

The solid level curves show \(q_A(x)=+1\); dashed curves show \(q_A(x)=-1\). The gray circle shows unit inputs. The zero set is shown separately when it has nonzero directions. These are **level sets of a scalar function**, not the image of the circle under A. Keep that distinction from Module 6's ellipse.

Try these experiments in order:

1. **Bowl:** keep λ₁=1 and λ₂=3. Move the probe to the shortest radius of q=1. Predict whether that axis has the smallest or largest eigenvalue, then reveal the principal axes.
2. **Rotate:** change only the axis angle. The level curves rotate and the directional trace shifts sideways. Its minimum and maximum stay the same. Entries of A change while its spectrum stays fixed.
3. **Flat valley:** set λ₂=0. The q=1 contour becomes two parallel lines, and the zero set is the whole flat axis. A vanished eigenvalue does not create an ellipse with radius zero; its radius has escaped to infinity.
4. **Saddle:** set λ₂=−1. Find a probe where R=0. Compare the zero height reading with the residual. A cancellation direction need not be a null direction.
5. **Isotropic:** make both eigenvalues equal. The trace becomes horizontal. Every direction is an eigenvector; the displayed pair of axes is merely one possible choice.
6. **Zero:** set both eigenvalues to zero. The zero set is the entire plane and both ±1 contours are empty. A blank contour plot here has a mathematical meaning, which the readout names.

For a probe at angle φ and a first eigenaxis at angle θ, the linked trace is

$$
R(\varphi)=\lambda_1\cos^2(\varphi-\theta)+\lambda_2\sin^2(\varphi-\theta).
$$

It repeats every 180°, because an arrow and its negative give the same measurement. The laboratory also reports the first Cholesky pivot a₁₁ and, when it is positive, the second pivot a₂₂−a₁₂²/a₁₁. Watch where the factorization stops as the bowl flattens. The geometric classification uses the controlled eigenvalues; rounded matrix entries and computed pivots are numerical readouts.

> **Practice — Foundation:** In the bowl preset (λ₁=1, λ₂=3, axis angle θ), evaluate R(φ) at φ=θ, θ+45°, and θ+90°, then give the minimum and maximum readings without changing either eigenvalue.
>
> **Hint:** Use \(R(\varphi)=\lambda_1\cos^2(\varphi-\theta)+\lambda_2\sin^2(\varphi-\theta)\). The value depends on angle relative to the axes, so the extremes sit on the principal axes.
>
> **Practice — Core:** For A=diag(1,4), find the distance from the origin to the contour xᵀAx=1 along e₁ and along e₂. Explain why the long axis of the q=1 ellipse belongs to the smaller positive eigenvalue.
>
> **Hint:** Along a unit eigenvector, q(tq_i)=λ_i t². Solve for the distance t needed to reach height one.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** In the saddle preset (λ₁=1, λ₂=−1) with axis angle 0, so A=diag(1,−1), find the two zero-value lines of q and check that they are perpendicular. Compute A(1,1). Why is neither line the null space?
>
> **Hint:** q(x)=x₁²−x₂² vanishes exactly on x₂=±x₁. A(1,1)=(1,−1)≠0, and both eigenvalues are nonzero, so A is invertible.

## 5. Read a quadratic form from its signs

For any real square A, the scalar xᵀAx equals its own transpose. Therefore

$$
x^{\mathsf T}Ax=x^{\mathsf T}\left(\frac{A+A^{\mathsf T}}2\right)x.
$$

Only the symmetric part contributes. The skew-symmetric part (A−Aᵀ)/2 contributes zero for every x. You may symmetrize to study a quadratic form, but that changes the linear map and can change its spectrum. For [[1,4],[0,1]], both eigenvalues are 1, yet its symmetric part [[1,2],[2,1]] has eigenvalues −1 and 3: the quadratic form takes both signs.

From now on A is symmetric. Eigen-coordinates eliminate all cross terms:

$$
q_A(x)=\lambda_1y_1^2+\cdots+\lambda_ny_n^2.
$$

| Eigenvalue signs | Name | What q does on nonzero inputs |
|---|---|---|
| All positive | Positive definite (PD) | Strictly positive |
| All nonnegative | Positive semidefinite (PSD) | Nonnegative; zero directions possible |
| All negative | Negative definite | Strictly negative |
| All nonpositive | Negative semidefinite | Nonpositive; zero directions possible |
| At least one positive and one negative | Indefinite | Takes both signs |

PD is a special case of PSD. The zero matrix is both positive and negative semidefinite. “Singular” is a rank statement; a singular form can still be indefinite in dimension three or more, for example diag(1,−1,0).

In two dimensions, positive eigenvalues give an ellipse at q=c>0 with semiaxis lengths √(c/λᵢ). Opposite signs give hyperbolas at nonzero levels; the zero level consists of two intersecting lines. For diag(λ,0), λ>0, q=c>0 is two parallel lines, q=0 is one line, and negative levels are empty. For a negative definite form the analogous ellipses occur at negative levels. In a positive definite form q=0 contains only the origin.

**A stronger zero statement needs a sign hypothesis.** For PSD A,

$$
x^{\mathsf T}Ax=0\iff Ax=0.
$$

Every λᵢyᵢ² is nonnegative, so a zero sum forces yᵢ=0 wherever λᵢ>0. That is exactly the condition Λy=0. For an indefinite form, cancellation breaks the inference.

A general coordinate substitution x=Ty changes the form to yᵀ(TᵀAT)y. This is **congruence**, not the similarity T⁻¹AT that describes the operator in new coordinates. They coincide for orthogonal T. General congruence need not preserve eigenvalues: I becomes diag(4,1) under T=diag(2,1). It does preserve the counts of positive, negative, and zero eigenvalues, called the **inertia**. To see why, the number of positive eigenvalues is the largest dimension of a subspace on which q is positive definite: the positive eigenspace attains it, and a larger subspace must meet the nonpositive eigenspace. Invertible T preserves such dimensions; apply the same reasoning to negative directions, then subtract from n for the zero count.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Classify diag(2,0,−1). Is singular the same as semidefinite?
>
> **Hint:** Test the first and third coordinate vectors separately. A zero eigenvalue does not erase the other two signs.
>
> **Practice — Core:** Prove that PSD plus xᵀAx=0 implies Ax=0, then give an indefinite counterexample.
>
> **Hint:** Use a sum of nonnegative eigen-coordinate terms for the proof. Use diag(1,−1) and equal coordinates for the counterexample.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Find the symmetric part of [[1,4],[0,1]] and a direction where its quadratic form is negative, despite the original matrix's positive eigenvalues.
>
> **Hint:** Try x=(1,−1). Symmetrizing preserves xᵀAx but does not preserve the original matrix's eigenvalues.

## 6. Positive definite means an invertible change of lengths

**Theorem 25 — equivalent certificates of positive definiteness.** For real symmetric A, these are equivalent:

- xᵀAx>0 for every x≠0;
- all eigenvalues are strictly positive;
- A=BᵀB for some invertible square B.

*Proof.* The eigen-coordinate sum proves the first equivalence, including necessity by testing eigenvectors. If λᵢ>0, let B=Λ¹ᐟ²Qᵀ; then BᵀB=A and B is invertible. Conversely, xᵀBᵀBx=‖Bx‖²>0 for x≠0 when B is invertible.

This also constructs the symmetric positive definite square root A¹ᐟ²=QΛ¹ᐟ²Qᵀ. The factor B above and the symmetric square root are different matrices, both providing squared-length representations. For PSD A the same construction works with zero eigenvalues, but the square root is singular and some lengths collapse.

Every Gram matrix XᵀX is PSD because vᵀXᵀXv=‖Xv‖². It is PD exactly when X has independent columns. Thus Module 3's metric xᵀGy is an inner product precisely when symmetric G is PD: xᵀGx supplies a strictly positive squared length. A semidefinite G is insufficient because distinct vectors can be distance zero apart.

The spectral bounds also say

$$
\lambda_1\|x\|^2\le x^{\mathsf T}Ax\le\lambda_n\|x\|^2.
$$

For PD A, λ₁ is the weakest stiffness. As it approaches zero, motion in that direction becomes cheaper; inverse eigenvalues 1/λᵢ grow. That is the geometric seed of conditioning, which Module 9 develops quantitatively.

**Two tempting shortcuts fail.** Positive diagonal entries are only coordinate-axis tests. The symmetric matrix [[1,2],[2,1]] has positive diagonal but is indefinite. Positive determinant says the product of eigenvalues is positive: −I in two dimensions passes that test and is negative definite. A finite collection of random positive directional readings is also not a proof of PD; it can miss a narrow set of negative directions.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Show that X=[[1,1],[2,2]] gives a PSD Gram matrix, and supply one nonzero vector with zero Gram length.
>
> **Hint:** A null vector of X is also a zero-length vector for XᵀX. The two columns are equal.
>
> **Practice — Core:** For diag(1,9), give its symmetric PD square root and the semiaxis lengths of xᵀAx=1.
>
> **Hint:** Square roots of eigenvalues build the factor; reciprocal square roots build the contour radii.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Show that positive diagonal plus positive determinant forces a symmetric 2×2 matrix to be PD. Then show it fails in 3D for \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&2\\2&1&2\\2&2&1\end{pmatrix}\) by computing det A and xᵀAx at x=(1,−1,0).
>
> **Hint:** In 2D complete the square using a₁₁>0. For the 3×3 matrix, write A=2·11ᵀ−I to read its eigenvalues, then evaluate the form at (1,−1,0) directly.

## 7. Cholesky: pay for one square at a time

Eigenvalues explain positive definiteness; a Cholesky factorization usually tests it more directly for a dense symmetric matrix. We seek a lower-triangular L with **positive diagonal** such that A=LLᵀ.

Start with A=[[a,b],[b,c]]. Completing the square gives

$$
ax_1^2+2bx_1x_2+cx_2^2
=a\left(x_1+\frac ba x_2\right)^2
+\left(c-\frac{b^2}{a}\right)x_2^2\quad(a>0).
$$

The second pivot c−b²/a is what remains after paying for the first square. Hence

$$
L=\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt a&0\\b/\sqrt a&\sqrt{c-b^2/a}\end{pmatrix}.
$$

For A=[[4,2],[2,3]], L=[[2,0],[1,√2]]. For [[1,2],[2,1]], the first pivot is 1 but the second is −3. The two positive diagonal entries could not pay for the coupling between coordinates.

**Theorem 26 — Cholesky criterion.** A real symmetric matrix is PD exactly when it admits A=LLᵀ with lower-triangular L and positive diagonal. That L is unique.

*Proof.* For a PD block matrix

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}a&r^{\mathsf T}\\r&C\end{pmatrix},
$$

a>0 by testing e₁. For any nonzero z, insert x=(−rᵀz/a,z) into xᵀAx. Positivity gives zᵀ(C−rrᵀ/a)z>0. The remaining symmetric matrix is therefore PD. Inductively factor it as MMᵀ, then set L=[[√a,0],[r/√a,M]]. Multiplication verifies LLᵀ=A. Conversely, positive triangular diagonal makes L invertible, and xᵀAx=‖Lᵀx‖²>0 for x≠0. The first column of L is forced by √a and r/√a, and induction forces the remaining block, proving uniqueness.

Matching entries gives the implementation, with j increasing and i>j:

$$
p_j=a_{jj}-\sum_{k<j}l_{jk}^2,\quad
l_{jj}=\sqrt{p_j},\quad
l_{ij}=\frac{a_{ij}-\sum_{k<j}l_{ik}l_{jk}}{l_{jj}}.
$$

In exact arithmetic, a nonpositive pivot stops this positive-diagonal factorization. A zero pivot may represent a valid PSD matrix; it still fails the **PD** test. Some PSD matrices admit triangular factors with zero diagonal, but those require separate handling and are outside this task. Do not take an absolute value inside the square root or silently add a diagonal shift to make the test pass: either changes the claim.

For a small 2×2, a>0 and det(A)>0 are equivalent to positive pivots because p₂=det(A)/a. In general, Cholesky gives the **leading principal minor criterion**: A is PD iff the determinants of its top-left k×k blocks are positive for every k. Necessity follows by restricting to coordinate subspaces; sufficiency follows inductively from the block determinant det(A)=a det(C−rrᵀ/a), applied to each leading block. Computing all those determinants is not the algorithm we recommend. Nonnegative *leading* minors alone do not characterize PSD: diag(0,−1) has leading determinants 0,0 but is not PSD.

**Our numerical contract.** The coding labs require entries to be exactly symmetric after conversion to floats; they do not silently average unequal triangles. They reject a computed pivot p_j≤tol·s, where s=max|aᵢⱼ| and tol>0. This scale-relative cutoff avoids calling a tiny multiple of I indefinite merely because its units are small. It can still reject an exactly PD matrix with a small pivot relative to s. A failed threshold test means **not accepted at this tolerance**, not a proof of a negative eigenvalue. A successful factorization is numerical evidence: audit LLᵀ−A as well. No arbitrary tolerance makes floating-point arithmetic an exact definiteness oracle.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Compute the two pivots and L for [[4,2],[2,3]].
>
> **Hint:** The off-diagonal factor is 2/√4=1; subtract its square from the second diagonal entry.
>
> **Practice — Core:** In the block proof take A=[[4,2],[2,3]], so a=4 and r=2. Set x=(−rz/a, z)=(−z/2, z) and evaluate xᵀAx. Why is the first coordinate chosen as −rᵀz/a?
>
> **Hint:** You should get 2z², the Schur complement 3−2²/4 times z². The choice makes the completed first square zero, isolating the remaining quadratic form on z.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** At tol=10⁻¹², compare the lab's decisions on 10⁻¹⁴I and diag(1,10⁻¹⁴). Are either matrices mathematically non-PD?
>
> **Hint:** Compute s separately for each matrix. The test compares a pivot to a relative scale, not to a universal absolute number.

## 8. Covariance, curvature, and a bounded bowl

**Covariance is a Gram story.** Let X contain m centered observation rows. Define the empirical covariance C=XᵀX/m (the alternative sample convention uses m−1 when m>1). For a direction v,

$$
v^{\mathsf T}Cv=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m(X_i v)^2.
$$

This is the average squared projected observation, so C is PSD. The Rayleigh maximum selects the unit direction of greatest empirical variance. Centering makes the rows sum to zero, so rank(X)≤m−1; if the number of features exceeds m−1, C cannot be PD. “Covariance matrix” does not promise an inverse. Module 8 develops PCA and the SVD from this starting point; probability supplies the population interpretation.

**An optimization problem without calculus.** Let f(x)=½xᵀAx−bᵀx with symmetric PD A, and solve Ax★=b. Expand around x★:

$$
f(x)=f(x_\star)+\frac12(x-x_\star)^{\mathsf T}A(x-x_\star).
$$

The linear terms cancel, so x★ is the unique global minimizer. With a Cholesky factor, solve Ly=b and then Lᵀx★=y; do not construct A⁻¹ just to apply it.

If A is PSD and singular, two different outcomes are possible. If b∈range(A), a solution exists and all minimizers form x★+ker(A). If b∉range(A), some z∈ker(A) has bᵀz≠0, since range(A)=ker(A)⊥ for symmetric A. Along tz the quadratic term vanishes and f(tz)=−t bᵀz is unbounded below in one direction. A flat direction is harmless only if the linear term does not tilt it. If A is indefinite, a negative eigenvector already gives an unbounded-below ray for this unconstrained quadratic, whatever b is.

**A calculus preview, with its assumptions.** For a twice continuously differentiable scalar loss, its Hessian H is symmetric and

$$
f(x+h)=f(x)+\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}h+\tfrac12h^{\mathsf T}H(x)h+o(\|h\|^2).
$$

Here the gradient contains first derivatives; the Hessian contains second derivatives; the final term divided by ‖h‖² tends to zero as h→0. At a stationary point (gradient zero), PD H gives a strict local minimum. Indefinite H gives a saddle. PSD H alone is inconclusive: x⁴+y⁴ has a strict minimum at the origin, while x⁴−y⁴ has a saddle, and both Hessians are zero there. Thus PD is a sufficient condition for a locally strict quadratic bowl, not a requirement for every optimizer or every minimum. See [calculus and optimization](../03-optimization/01-calculus-gradients-optimization.md) for the derivative arguments.

Finally, adding αI shifts every eigenvalue by α. A+αI is PD exactly when λ₁+α>0. A shift can repair a quadratic model, but it changes the model. In an implementation, record it rather than presenting the shifted matrix's factor as a factor of the original.

> **Practice — Foundation:** For \(X=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\\3&6\end{pmatrix}\), compute XᵀX and evaluate xᵀXᵀXx at x=(1,0) and x=(2,−1). Why is XᵀX PSD even though X is rectangular with dependent columns?
>
> **Hint:** Each value equals ‖Xx‖², a squared Euclidean norm. X(2,−1)=0 gives the zero value, so strict positivity fails exactly on the null space.
>
> **Practice — Core:** For A=diag(2,0), compare the minimizers of ½xᵀAx−bᵀx for b=(2,0) and b=(2,1).
>
> **Hint:** Write the function as x₁²−2x₁−b₂x₂. The second coordinate is either free or a direction of unlimited descent.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** For \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^4\) and \(g(x,y)=x^2-y^4\), compute the gradient and Hessian at the origin. Use them to refute the report “the Hessian is PSD, so this stationary point is a strict local minimum.”
>
> **Hint:** Both have zero gradient and Hessian diag(2,0) at the origin. Fourth-degree terms vanish from the Hessian but decide the behavior: compare f and g along the y-axis.

## Local numerical and research audit

### The complex-Hermitian analogue

Over complex coordinates replace transpose by conjugate transpose: \(\langle x,y\rangle=x^*y\). A Hermitian matrix satisfies \(H=H^*\); its quadratic form \(x^*Hx\) is real because it equals its complex conjugate. The spectral theorem becomes \(H=U\Lambda U^*\), with unitary \(U\) and real diagonal \(\Lambda\). Positive definiteness means \(x^*Hx>0\) for every nonzero complex \(x\).

For example, \(H=\begin{pmatrix}2&i\\-i&2\end{pmatrix}\) is Hermitian and has eigenvalues one and three. It is not real symmetric. This is the convention needed for later Fourier and complex spectral examples; replacing \(*\) by a plain transpose would lose the inner-product and positivity identities.

**M7 · Stretch · mixed — The complex-Hermitian analogue.** Compute the eigenvalues of H=[[2,i],[−i,2]] and determine whether H is positive definite.

## 9. Three runnable coding labs

All tasks use Python lists of rows and only the standard library. Preserve inputs and raise ValueError for malformed shapes, non-finite or boolean data. Shared validation helpers are supplied in the browser. These are small teaching algorithms; they are not a replacement for library factorizations on large or difficult arrays.

### Lab A — a directional meter

Open [Rayleigh quotient](../../labs/exercises.py). Implement `rayleigh_quotient(matrix, vector)` for a nonempty square matrix and matching nonzero vector. Return xᵀAx/(xᵀx), a scalar. Symmetry is **not required to compute the expression**; only our spectral interpretation requires it. Normalize x by its largest absolute entry and then its Euclidean length; likewise scale A by its largest absolute entry during the computation and restore the final units. This avoids squaring enormous original coordinates. A zero matrix returns zero; reject a non-finite final result. Compare proportional vectors, a saddle's zero reading, and a nonsymmetric input.

### Lab B — a constructive certificate

Open [Cholesky factorization](../../labs/exercises.py). Implement `cholesky(matrix, tol=1e-12)`, returning a full list-of-rows lower-triangular L with positive diagonal. Require exact symmetry of the validated entries and positive finite tol, excluding booleans. Use the recurrence in section 7, rejecting every computed pivot ≤tol·max|aᵢⱼ| with ValueError. The zero matrix must fail. Reject non-finite arithmetic as well. Reconstruct LLᵀ, and compare PD, indefinite, singular PSD, and small-scale PD inputs. A rejection must never be repaired by taking the square root of an absolute value.

### Lab C — a verdict with a stated scope

Open [positive-definiteness test](../../labs/exercises.py). Implement `is_pd(matrix, tol=1e-12)`. Return True exactly when the same pivot test accepts, and False for symmetric finite matrices it rejects on a pivot. Invalid data, nonsymmetry, invalid tolerance, or non-finite arithmetic must raise ValueError, not return False. The supplied `_validated_symmetric` helper checks input and tolerance; implement the pivot loop so mathematical rejection is distinguished from invalid arithmetic. A bare `except ValueError: return False` erases that distinction.

The name is convenient; its contract is a **numerical acceptance test**, not an exact yes/no theorem on arbitrary real data. At the default tolerance, diag(1,10⁻¹⁴) returns False even though it is PD. Decreasing tolerance can change the report and cannot remove roundoff. Document that distinction in your function.

Run `python -m labs.checks rayleigh-quotient`, `python -m labs.checks cholesky`, and `python -m labs.checks is-pd`. Add `--reference` after attempting your implementation to check the supplied solutions.

## 10. Exercises · by hand

**A1 · Foundation · paper — reciprocal entries.** For A=[[2,1],[1,3]], u=(1,0), and v=(0,1), compute uᵀAv and (Au)ᵀv. State the property these measurements illustrate.

**A2 · Core · paper — two rooms stay separate.** Prove that the orthogonal complement of an invariant subspace of a real symmetric matrix is invariant. Identify the step that fails for a nonsymmetric matrix.

**A3 · Core · paper — diagonalize a landscape.** For A=[[2,1],[1,2]], use q₁=(1,−1)/√2 and q₂=(1,1)/√2. Give the eigenvalues in that order, the eigen-coordinates of x=(2,0), and xᵀAx.

**A4 · Core · paper — weighted votes.** For A=diag(1,3) and x=(1,2), compute R_A(x) and the squared residual of the normalized vector. Is R_A(x) an eigenvalue?

**A5 · Core · paper — zero height is not zero image.** For A=diag(1,−1) and x=(1,1), compute xᵀAx and Ax. State an additional hypothesis under which zero quadratic value would imply zero image, and prove it.

**A6 · Foundation · paper — read the contour radii.** For A=diag(1,9), give the positive intercepts of xᵀAx=1 on the two coordinate axes. Which axis has greater stiffness?

**A7 · Core · paper — a determinant trap.** Give one symmetric 2×2 matrix with positive determinant that is not PD, and one with positive diagonal entries that is indefinite. Explain why each shortcut fails.

**A8 · Core · paper — complete the squares.** Compute the Cholesky pivots and lower-triangular factor for A=[[4,2],[2,3]]. Verify its product and express xᵀAx as a sum of two squares.

**A9 · Core · paper — invisible skew.** Find the symmetric part of A=[[1,4],[0,1]]. Give its ascending eigenvalues and evaluate xᵀAx at x=(1,−1). Why do A's own eigenvalues not classify this quadratic form?

**A10 · Stretch · paper — the middle eigenvalue without a polynomial.** For A=diag(1,4,9), prove min over all planes S of max over nonzero x in S of R_A(x)=4. Supply a plane attaining the minimum.

**A11 · Stretch · paper — existence before orthogonality.** Reconstruct the spectral theorem's maximum-on-the-sphere proof. Explain why proving distinct eigenvectors are orthogonal is not already a proof of the theorem.

**A12 · Stretch · paper — same inertia, different spectrum.** Let A=I₂ and T=diag(2,1). Compute TᵀAT and T⁻¹AT. Explain which describes a transformed quadratic form and why its eigenvalues can change without its inertia changing.

## 11. Exercises · NumPy

Use float64 arrays. `np.linalg.eigh` is the symmetric eigensolver. Check symmetry yourself before calling it: a routine that reads one triangle cannot validate agreement between both triangles for you. Compare equations, residuals, and subspaces rather than chosen eigenvector signs.

**B1 · Foundation · NumPy — audit the factorization.** Use `np.linalg.eigh` on [[2,1],[1,2]]. Report ascending eigenvalues, ‖AQ−QΛ‖, ‖QᵀQ−I‖, and ‖A−QΛQᵀ‖. Explain what each residual checks.

**B2 · Core · NumPy — a sweep is evidence.** Sample 721 equally spaced angles over one full turn for A=[[2,1],[1,2]]. Compare sampled Rayleigh extrema with eigenvalues; compute every eigen-coordinate weight. Repeat after rotating A by an arbitrary angle and explain why the sampled extrema need not be exact.

**B3 · Core · NumPy — test the threshold's meaning.** At tol=10⁻¹², compare your Cholesky acceptance on 10⁻¹⁴I₂, diag(1,10⁻¹⁴), [[1,1],[1,1]], and [[1,2],[2,1]]. Compare with library Cholesky and actual eigenvalues. Explain any different decisions without calling every rejection indefinite.

**B4 · Core · NumPy — covariance has a forced null direction.** Center the rows of X=[[1,0,2],[0,1,2],[1,1,4]]. Form C=XᵀX/3 after centering. Give its rank and one exact nonzero null direction. Verify that the Rayleigh maximum equals its largest eigenvalue.

**B5 · Stretch · NumPy — positive diagonal can hide a saddle.** For the 3×3 matrix with diagonal 1 and all off-diagonal entries 2, compute the ascending eigenvalues, determinant, and first two leading principal minors. Refute the rule “positive diagonal and determinant imply PD in every dimension.”

## 12. Exercises · PyTorch

**C1 · Foundation · PyTorch — a batch of landscapes.** In float64, use `torch.linalg.eigh` on a batch containing diag(1,3), diag(1,0), diag(1,−1), and the zero matrix. Classify each from all its eigenvalue signs; explain why a zero eigenvalue is not itself evidence of a saddle.

**C2 · Core · PyTorch — flat or tilted.** For A=diag(2,0), evaluate f(x)=½xᵀAx−bᵀx along x=(1,t), t=−10,0,10. Compare b=(2,0) and b=(2,1). Report both sequences and interpret the set of minimizers or absence of a lower bound.

**C3 · Core · PyTorch — shifts change the model.** For A=[[1,2],[2,1]], compare the eigenvalues after adding αI for α=0,1,1.1. Find the strict condition on α for PD, and explain why equality at the boundary is insufficient.

**C4 · Stretch · PyTorch — repeated axes are not identifiable.** For A=diag(1,1,4), rotate the first two columns of an orthonormal eigenbasis by angle 0.37. Verify both eigenbases, then compare their first columns and the projectors onto their first two columns. What should a regression test compare?

## 13. Derivations to own

1. Prove reciprocity, orthogonality of distinct eigenspaces, and invariance of orthogonal complements.
2. Find one eigenvector by a sphere maximum, then prove the spectral theorem inductively.
3. Derive the Rayleigh weighted-average and residual identities, the extreme bounds, and the k-dimensional min–max formula.
4. Classify quadratic forms from eigenvalue signs; explain the PSD-only implication from zero value to null vector.
5. Prove the Gram and Cholesky characterizations of PD; derive the pivot recurrence by matching entries.
6. Complete the square for an unconstrained quadratic, including the flat-direction compatibility condition.

## 14. Exercises · cumulative

**M1 · Core · paper — projection already knows the theorem.** Let P be the orthogonal projector onto span((1,1)). Give its matrix and ascending eigenvalues. Express xᵀPx as a squared length; classify I−P and identify its null space.

**M2 · Core · paper — QR predicts Cholesky.** If X has independent columns and thin QR factorization X=QR with positive diagonal R, prove XᵀX=RᵀR. Which matrix is the Cholesky factor? Explain why this identity is not an instruction to solve least squares through normal equations.

**M3 · Core · paper — solve a bowl.** For A=[[4,2],[2,3]] and b=(6,5), use two triangular solves to find the minimizer of ½xᵀAx−bᵀx. Give the minimum value and prove uniqueness without differentiation.

**M4 · Core · paper — recurrence with symmetry.** For symmetric A with all eigenvalues of magnitude at most 0.8, prove ‖Aᵏx‖≤0.8ᵏ‖x‖. Explain why the transient amplification from Module 6 cannot occur under this hypothesis.

**M5 · Stretch · paper — a metric changes symmetry's entry test.** Let G be symmetric PD and GA=AᵀG. Prove B=G¹ᐟ²AG⁻¹ᐟ² is symmetric, deduce real eigenvalues for A, and explain how to choose its eigenvectors G-orthonormally.

**M6 · Stretch · mixed — a covariance audit.** A centered dataset has five observations and eight features. A report claims its empirical covariance has eight strictly positive eigenvalues, “because every feature has nonzero variance.” Give the largest possible rank and smallest possible nullity, and explain what to inspect in the report.

## 15. Exercises · checkpoint

**K1 · Foundation · gate — read the axes.** For A=[[3,1],[1,3]], give ascending eigenvalues, one orthonormal eigenbasis, and the long and short semiaxis lengths of xᵀAx=1. Explain the inverse relation between radius and eigenvalue.

**K2 · Core · gate — defend the geometric guarantee.** Prove the real spectral theorem, naming the existence fact used and explaining how the induction preserves symmetry. State why repeated eigenvalues cause no defect.

**K3 · Core · gate — diagnose three zero readings.** Compare A=diag(1,−1) at x=(1,1), B=diag(1,0) at x=(0,1), and C=0 at any nonzero x. Each has zero quadratic value. Give the images and explain which zero sets are null spaces.

**K4 · Core · gate — construct and audit a certificate.** Factor A=[[9,3],[3,2]] by Cholesky, giving its pivots and L. Explain exactly what this certifies in exact arithmetic, and what extra qualifications accompany a floating-point, tolerance-based test.

**K5 · Stretch · gate — a bounded optimization claim.** For A=diag(2,0), decide whether f(x)=½xᵀAx−bᵀx has a minimizer for b=(4,0) and b=(4,1). Give every minimizer or a direction showing unboundedness. State the general PSD compatibility criterion.

**K6 · Stretch · gate — recover a missing axis variationally.** A symmetric 3×3 matrix has ascending eigenvalues 1,4,9. Without choosing its entries, prove that every plane contains a nonzero vector of Rayleigh quotient at least 4 and that some plane has no quotient greater than 4. If a unit probe has R=3.9 and residual norm 0.2, what eigenvalue-proximity statement is justified? Does that alone identify a unique signed eigenvector?

## Mastery check

Given an unfamiliar symmetric matrix, connect an orthonormal basis, directional readings, contour geometry, eigenvalue signs, and a constructive PD test. Show why each conclusion follows, and identify the exact point where it would fail without symmetry or definiteness. Keep exact theorems, sampled plots, and tolerance-based decisions separate.

**What to bring to Module 8:** a symmetric Gram matrix is PSD; its null directions are the original map's null directions; and its orthonormal eigenvectors separate squared lengths. The SVD will use those facts to describe rectangular maps, then make low-rank approximation and PCA precise.

# The SVD — geometry, rank, low-rank approximation and PCA

You have a machine with a thousand input coordinates and a hundred output coordinates. Someone asks you to replace it with a cheaper machine that can transmit only five independent signals. Which five? What information disappears? And when would “almost all the energy retained” still be a bad answer?

The singular value decomposition gives a precise language for that negotiation. It finds perpendicular input directions that the machine sends to perpendicular output directions. Each direction gets its own nonnegative gain. Keeping only some of those paired directions produces an approximation whose error we can calculate—and, for two important error measures, prove optimal.

## 0. The route through the chapter

Five results carry the work: every real matrix has an SVD; its paired directions reveal the four fundamental subspaces; its singular values measure worst-case and total squared amplification; truncation gives a best rank-constrained approximation; and PCA is that same approximation problem applied to centered observations.

We work over the reals. Let A be m×n, p=min(m,n), and r=rank(A). Singular values are in **descending** order, σ₁≥⋯≥σₚ≥0. This reverses Module 7's ascending eigenvalue convention. Input vectors live in ℝⁿ; output vectors live in ℝᵐ. Keeping those two spaces separate is the first conceptual step.

Sections 1–10 build the ideas and experiments; section 11 supplies three runnable stdlib Python tasks. Local NumPy and PyTorch exercises follow. Thirty-four hours includes derivations, coding, and unfamiliar problems, not merely reading. We introduce only the two matrix norms needed for approximation; Module 9 develops general norms and conditioning, and Module 10 develops the pseudoinverse and regularization in full.

## 1. Two spaces need two sets of directions

An eigenvector asks for Av=λv. That compares an output to its own input, so it requires a square matrix acting on the same space. Even then, a real eigenbasis may not exist. An SVD asks a different question:

> Can we find perpendicular inputs whose outputs are also perpendicular?

If so, the map can be understood as independent channels, each with an input direction vᵢ, an output direction uᵢ, and a gain σᵢ:

$$
Av_i=\sigma_i u_i.
$$

The left and right vectors are unit vectors in different spaces. A sign reversal is carried by the directions, allowing σᵢ≥0. An input direction that the map kills has gain zero; we must not try to normalize its zero output into an output direction.

**A rectangular machine you can see completely.** Consider

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}3&0&0\\0&2&0\end{pmatrix}.
$$

It sends e₁∈ℝ³ to 3e₁∈ℝ², e₂ to 2e₂, and e₃ to zero. Its rank is 2. Its two listed singular values are 3 and 2, both positive, yet its null space is nontrivial. There are three input directions and only two output directions; the extra null direction is carried by the **full input basis**, not by an extra entry in a length-two singular-value list.

**An eigenvalue trap.** For the shear A=[[1,2],[0,1]], both eigenvalues are 1. But Ae₂=(2,1) has length √5. The eigenvalues did not bound one-step stretching, because the shear's behavior is not expressed in an orthonormal eigenbasis. Its singular values will answer that length question.

Before going on, say aloud which space each symbol belongs to: x and vᵢ are inputs, Ax and uᵢ are outputs. An SVD does not generally make vᵢ and uᵢ the same arrow.

## 2. Construct the SVD from one symmetric matrix

**Theorem 27 — singular value decomposition.** Every real m×n matrix can be written

$$
A=U\Sigma V^{\mathsf T},
$$

where U is m×m orthogonal, V is n×n orthogonal, and Σ is an m×n matrix whose only possibly nonzero entries are σᵢ in positions (i,i), in descending order. Exactly r of them are positive.

*Proof, starting in input space.* The Gram matrix AᵀA is symmetric PSD because xᵀAᵀAx=‖Ax‖². Module 7 gives an orthonormal eigenbasis v₁,…,vₙ and nonnegative eigenvalues. Order the positive ones first, and write them as σᵢ². For each positive σᵢ define

$$
u_i=\frac{Av_i}{\sigma_i}.
$$

These vectors are orthonormal:

$$
u_i^{\mathsf T}u_j
=\frac{v_i^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}Av_j}{\sigma_i\sigma_j}
=\frac{\sigma_j^2}{\sigma_i\sigma_j}\,v_i^{\mathsf T}v_j
=\begin{cases}1&i=j,\\0&i\ne j.\end{cases}
$$

If vᵢ belongs to a zero eigenvalue of AᵀA, then ‖Avᵢ‖²=0, hence Avᵢ=0. Thus the images of the positive directions span range(A), and there are r of them. Complete u₁,…,uᵣ to an orthonormal basis of ℝᵐ using Module 4's basis-extension machinery. Complete V with the zero-eigenvalue directions already obtained. Every column of AV agrees with the corresponding column of UΣ, so AV=UΣ and A=UΣVᵀ.

The proof never assumes A is square, invertible, symmetric, or diagonalizable. It also explains why the division by σᵢ occurs only for positive values.

For i≤r we additionally have

$$
A^{\mathsf T}u_i=\sigma_i v_i,\qquad
AA^{\mathsf T}u_i=\sigma_i^2u_i.
$$

The first equation follows by substituting uᵢ=Avᵢ/σᵢ, and the second by applying A. Positive eigenvalues of AᵀA and AAᵀ therefore match, including multiplicities; their extra zero eigenvalues depend on n and m.

**An existence proof is not automatically a numerical algorithm.** Forming AᵀA squares singular values, making small directions harder to resolve amid rounding. For example, with A=[[1,1],[0,ε]], its determinant is ε, so it is full rank whenever ε≠0. Yet the Gram entry 1+ε² can round to 1, erasing that distinction. Production SVD routines work with A directly rather than using this proof as a recipe. Our 2×2 teaching task uses Gram geometry with explicitly limited numerical claims.

## 3. Read, scale, write—and distinguish an image from a contour

For any input x, compute c=Vᵀx, then Σc, then UΣc. These are three different actions:

1. **Read** x in a perpendicular input basis.
2. **Scale** the retained coordinates, killing zero-gain coordinates and inserting any necessary output zeros.
3. **Write** the result in a perpendicular output basis.

The orthogonal maps can include reflections. For a rectangular map, the middle operation also changes dimension. “Rotate, scale, rotate” is a useful picture only if those qualifications remain attached.

Toggle the rank-one approximation to see exactly what deleting the second channel changes. Reveal the axes after predicting them.

For an isotropic map the gains coincide, so any perpendicular input pair can be used: a returned axis is not a uniquely discovered feature. The thin preset has a small positive second gain; changing the displayed rank tolerance changes its reported numerical rank without changing A.

**Do not swap these two ellipses.** The image of the unit circle under diag(3,1) has semiaxes 3 and 1. The level set xᵀdiag(9,1)x=1 has semiaxes 1/3 and 1. The image asks “where do unit inputs go?” The level set asks “which inputs have unit output length?” One uses gains, the other reciprocal gains.

An SVD is not fully unique. For a positive channel you may change the signs of uᵢ and vᵢ together. Inside a repeated positive singular-value block you may rotate the input basis and output basis by the same orthogonal matrix. Null-space bases can be chosen independently. Check reconstructions, paired equations, and subspace projectors; do not demand one particular collection of signed arrows.

## 4. Shapes, subspaces, and the channels that disappear

Three forms of the factorization are useful. They encode the same map but expose different amounts of unused geometry.

| Form | U factor | Middle factor | Vᵀ factor | What is retained |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Full | m×m | m×n | n×n | Complete input and output bases |
| Reduced, also called economy | m×p | p×p | p×n | p=min(m,n) paired slots, including any zero gains |
| Compact rank-r | m×r | r×r | r×n | Only positive-gain channels |

Software terminology varies; inspect shapes rather than inferring them from the word “thin.” For the 2×3 example, reduced Vᵀ is 2×3 and omits the extra input null vector. For a rank-one example, reduced factors also contain a zero-gain slot, whereas compact rank-r factors do not.

**Theorem 28 — four subspaces from the full factors.** With positive channels first,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{range}(A)&=\operatorname{span}(u_1,\ldots,u_r),&
\ker(A^{\mathsf T})&=\operatorname{span}(u_{r+1},\ldots,u_m),\\
\operatorname{range}(A^{\mathsf T})&=\operatorname{span}(v_1,\ldots,v_r),&
\ker(A)&=\operatorname{span}(v_{r+1},\ldots,v_n).
\end{aligned}
$$

*Proof.* Write x=Vc. Since U preserves length, Ax=0 iff Σc=0, exactly when the first r coordinates vanish. Every output is a combination of u₁,…,uᵣ, and each such uᵢ is the output of vᵢ/σᵢ. Apply the same argument to Aᵀ=VΣᵀUᵀ for the other two spaces.

Consequently the orthogonal range projector is UᵣUᵣᵀ and the row-space projector is VᵣVᵣᵀ. These survive changes of basis inside their respective subspaces.

**Exact rank and a numerical report are different objects.** Exact rank counts positive singular values. A numerical rank rule might count σᵢ>τ·σ₁ for a declared relative τ≥0. With A=diag(1,10⁻⁸), exact rank is 2; at τ=10⁻⁶ that rule reports 1. The matrix has not changed. The report states which channels the chosen resolution treats as usable. Units, measurement noise, dtype, and the downstream task should inform that resolution; there is no context-free threshold that discovers exact rank from rounded data.

**A bridge to minimum-norm solutions.** If Ax=b is consistent, the positive-channel coordinates are forced to be

$$
c_i=\frac{u_i^{\mathsf T}b}{\sigma_i}\quad(i\le r).
$$

Coordinates in ker(A) are free. Since V is orthogonal, setting all free coordinates to zero uniquely minimizes ‖x‖. For inconsistent b, first project b onto range(A); the same formula then gives the least-squares solution of minimum norm, with residual b−UᵣUᵣᵀb. This is the SVD reason behind the minimum-norm claim used in optimization. Module 10 defines the pseudoinverse operator and investigates what small σᵢ do to this division.

## 5. Two error measures, two precise promises

For a matrix E, the **spectral norm** is its greatest amplification of a unit vector:

$$
\|E\|_2=\max_{\|x\|=1}\|Ex\|.
$$

The **Frobenius norm** is the ordinary Euclidean length of all its entries taken together:

$$
\|E\|_F^2=\sum_{i,j}e_{ij}^2=\sum_j\|Ee_j\|^2.
$$

The first measures worst-case error on a unit input; the second measures total squared entrywise error, equivalently the sum of squared output errors on the coordinate basis. Both are unchanged by orthogonal transformations on either side. Left invariance preserves each output length. Right invariance follows for the spectral norm because an orthogonal map permutes the unit sphere, and for the Frobenius norm by applying length preservation to each row.

**Theorem 29 — gains determine amplification and energy.** The SVD gives

$$
\|A\|_2=\sigma_1,\qquad
\|A\|_F^2=\sum_{i=1}^p\sigma_i^2.
$$

*Proof.* For a unit x=Vc, ‖Ax‖²=∑ᵢ₌₁ʳσᵢ²cᵢ²≤σ₁². Choosing x=v₁ attains the bound when A is nonzero; the zero case is immediate. Orthogonal invariance reduces the Frobenius norm to that of Σ, which has only its singular values as nonzero entries.

For a rectangular map, the **minimum** over all unit inputs is zero whenever r<n. It need not be σₚ: a wide full-row-rank matrix has positive σₚ but omitted null directions. On the row space, the smallest positive gain is σᵣ when r>0.

There is a useful isotropic-input interpretation. If a random input has mean zero and E[xxᵀ]=I, then expanding coordinates gives

$$
\mathbb E\|Ex\|^2=\|E\|_F^2.
$$

If instead x is uniform on the unit sphere in ℝⁿ, its second moment is I/n, so the average is ‖E‖_F²/n. Anisotropic inputs weight errors differently. We will use that distinction to avoid claiming that a matrix approximation automatically preserves a model's behavior.

## 6. A rank budget means choosing channels

The SVD also writes a matrix as a sum of rank-one maps:

$$
A=\sum_{i=1}^r\sigma_i u_i v_i^{\mathsf T}.
$$

Each term reads the scalar vᵢᵀx, multiplies by σᵢ, and writes along uᵢ. Retaining the first k slots, with 0≤k≤p, gives

$$
A_k=\sum_{i=1}^k\sigma_i u_i v_i^{\mathsf T},\qquad
\operatorname{rank}(A_k)\le k.
$$

If k≥r then A_k=A. If k=0, the empty sum is the zero matrix. The residual simply contains the discarded channels. Define σₚ₊₁=0; then

$$
\|A-A_k\|_2=\sigma_{k+1},\qquad
\|A-A_k\|_F^2=\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2.
$$

These equations already predict the whole error curve. But why should this choice beat *every* rank-k matrix, including ones assembled from entirely different directions?

**Theorem 30 — Eckart–Young, spectral and Frobenius forms.** Among all matrices B with rank at most k, A_k minimizes both displayed errors.

*Spectral proof.* For k<p, restrict B to S=span(v₁,…,vₖ₊₁). Since S has dimension k+1 but B has rank at most k, there is a unit x∈S with Bx=0. Therefore

$$
\|A-B\|_2\ge\|(A-B)x\|=\|Ax\|\ge\sigma_{k+1}.
$$

A_k attains the bound. For k=p, A itself is available and has zero error.

*Frobenius proof.* Let P be the orthogonal projector onto range(B), of dimension d≤k. Columnwise orthogonality gives

$$
\|A-B\|_F^2
=\|(I-P)A\|_F^2+\|PA-B\|_F^2
\ge\|A\|_F^2-\|PA\|_F^2.
$$

Using the SVD, ‖PA‖_F²=∑ᵢ₌₁ʳσᵢ²‖Puᵢ‖². Extend this to all m left basis vectors by assigning zero weights beyond r. The numbers αᵢ=‖Puᵢ‖² lie in [0,1] and sum to d: in an orthonormal basis of range(P), expand each projected uᵢ and sum the squared dot products. A budget of d≤k units placed on descending nonnegative weights earns at most the sum of the largest k weights. Thus ‖PA‖_F²≤∑ᵢ≤kσᵢ², leaving at least ∑ᵢ>kσᵢ² error. A_k attains it.

The “budget” step is a small optimization argument: if some weight is placed on a smaller coefficient while a larger one is not filled, moving that amount upward cannot decrease the sum. Repeat until the largest coefficients are filled.

**Optimal does not always mean unique.** A tie across the cutoff lets different subspaces achieve the same best errors. For I₂ and k=1, any rank-one orthogonal projector is optimal. Even with a strict gap, spectral-norm minimizers need not be unique: for A=diag(3,1), both diag(3,0) and diag(2,0) attain spectral error 1, but their Frobenius errors differ. A strict positive cutoff gap does make the Frobenius-optimal truncation unique; the paired vectors within retained repeated blocks still need not be unique.

## 8. PCA chooses an affine subspace for observations

Let X be an N×d data matrix with observations in rows and features in columns. Let μ be the row vector of feature means, and define the centered matrix

$$
X_c=X-\mathbf1\mu.
$$

Centering matters because PCA describes variation around a location. Uncentered SVD instead approximates the data by a subspace through the origin, which may devote its leading direction mostly to the mean.

Take an SVD X_c=UΣVᵀ and choose 0≤k≤min(N,d). The columns vᵢ of V are **feature directions**, also called principal axes or loadings under a common convention. The projected observations are the **scores**

$$
Z_k=X_cV_k=U_k\Sigma_k\quad(N\times k).
$$

A loading is a direction in feature space; a score is one observation's coordinate along that direction. Unit entries of U are not the scores: they must be multiplied by singular values. The rank-k centered reconstruction and the reconstruction in original coordinates are

$$
\widehat X_c=Z_kV_k^{\mathsf T},\qquad
\widehat X=\mathbf1\mu+\widehat X_c.
$$

The reconstructed points lie in the **affine** space μ+span(v₁,…,v_k). The matrix with the mean added back can have rank k+1 even though its centered part has rank at most k.

**Theorem 31 — PCA's two equivalent objectives.** Among orthonormal d×k direction matrices Q, choosing V_k maximizes projected squared variation ‖X_cQ‖_F² and minimizes reconstruction error ‖X_c−X_cQQᵀ‖_F².

*Proof.* Projection splits each centered observation into perpendicular kept and discarded parts, so their squared lengths add. Hence minimizing residual energy is equivalent to maximizing projected energy. The spectral theorem applied to X_cᵀX_c, with the same projection-weight budget argument used in section 6, shows that the top k right singular directions maximize that energy. Equivalently, SVD truncation is an optimal rank-k approximation and has the required projection form. Its squared residual is ∑ᵢ>kσᵢ².

Why place the affine subspace at μ? For any candidate location a and projector P=QQᵀ, sum the squared orthogonal distances. Writing xⱼ−a=(xⱼ−μ)+(μ−a), the cross terms sum to zero because centered rows sum to zero. The result is

$$
\sum_j\|(I-P)(x_j-a)\|^2
=\sum_j\|(I-P)(x_j-\mu)\|^2
+N\|(I-P)(\mu-a)\|^2.
$$

Thus an optimum passes through the mean. The choice of a along the same affine subspace is immaterial.

For N>1, the sample covariance C=X_cᵀX_c/(N−1) has eigenvalues λᵢ=σᵢ²/(N−1), with extra zeros if needed. The **explained-variance ratio** is

$$
\frac{\sigma_i^2}{\sum_j\sigma_j^2},
$$

provided the denominator is positive. The covariance divisor cancels in the ratio. Centering also forces rank(X_c)≤min(N−1,d), so a dataset with fewer observations than features has unavoidable zero-variance directions.

$$

The excess above optimal is explicit. This is a useful prediction test for the lab: a 45° line should cost 5, even before pressing reveal.

> **Practice — Foundation:** For the hand-checkable dataset, list the first principal-component scores using the positive horizontal direction.
>
> **Hint:** Subtract the mean and take each row's dot product with (1,0).
>
> **Practice — Core:** Compute the reconstruction error for the 45° candidate and compare it with the best horizontal line.
>
> **Hint:** Substitute sin²45°=1/2 into the derived excess-error formula.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** For three coincident observations X=[[3,5],[3,5],[3,5]], center the data, then compute the rank-one reconstruction error and the leading explained-variance ratio. Why is the first zero and the second undefined?
>
> **Hint:** Every centered observation is zero. The error is a sum of zeros; the fraction divides zero by zero.

## 10. Scaling and whitening change what counts as a good picture

PCA minimizes Euclidean reconstruction error in the supplied coordinates. Changing a feature from meters to millimeters multiplies that coordinate by 1000 and its squared errors by a million. The fitted direction can change even when the underlying measurements describe the same objects.

Standardizing each nonconstant feature to sample variance one makes a different choice: distances are measured in feature-standard-deviation units. It can be appropriate when those units match the question, but it can also amplify an unreliable low-variance feature. A constant feature cannot be standardized by dividing by its zero standard deviation. State how you handle it.

**Whitening goes further.** If the k retained covariance eigenvalues are positive, define

$$
W=X_cV_k\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1^{-1/2},\ldots,\lambda_k^{-1/2}).
$$

With our sample covariance convention, WᵀW/(N−1)=I_k. Since λᵢ=σᵢ²/(N−1), this also equals √(N−1)U_k. Whitening rotates and rescales; PCA projection alone only changes the represented directions and discards others. In the retained space, squared distance between two rows becomes a sum of squared score differences divided by the respective λᵢ, so weak-variance directions receive more weight.

Zero variance cannot be inverted. Tiny estimated variance can turn small errors into large whitened coordinates. Truncating directions or adding a positive variance floor are modeling choices that change the transformation. They should be named, not hidden inside a square root. Module 10 develops spectral regularization, and [high-dimensional probability](../05-probability-statistics/12-high-dimensional-probability.md) examines statistical uncertainty in empirical spectra.

**A final inference check.** PCA's optimality says nothing about labels, causes, or semantic importance. A low-variance direction can predict a target perfectly. A high-variance direction can encode an irrelevant nuisance. Fitting a transform on held-out observations also uses information from those observations; evaluation pipelines should estimate centering, scaling, and principal directions on training data, then apply the fixed transform to held-out data.

What is a decaying spectrum evidence for? A good low-rank approximation **under a stated norm and coordinates**. To claim preserved task behavior, measure it on relevant inputs. To claim a uniquely identified component, inspect the spectral gaps. To claim a usable inverse transformation, inspect discarded and tiny directions.

> **Practice — Foundation:** For covariance eigenvalues (9,1), what factors multiply the two PCA score coordinates during whitening?
>
> **Hint:** Use inverse square roots of covariance eigenvalues, not inverse singular values without the sample-size factor.
>
> **Practice — Core:** For X=[[1,5],[3,5],[5,5]], compute each feature's sample variance. Explain why neither standardization nor whitening may silently divide by the second feature's standard deviation.
>
> **Hint:** The second column is constant, so its variance is 0 and the scaling 1/0 is undefined. Dropping that direction or using a floor is an explicit change of the transform.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Let y=±1 with equal probability, \(x_1\sim N(0,100)\) independent of y, and \(x_2=0.1y\). Compute the variances of x₁ and x₂, the first principal direction, and which coordinate predicts y. What does this show about keeping only top-variance directions?
>
> **Hint:** The covariance is diag(100, 0.01), so the first principal direction is e₁. Yet x₁ is an independent nuisance, while sign(x₂) equals y exactly.

## Local numerical and research audit

### Compare subspaces and evaluate PCA out of sample

Repeated singular values identify a subspace without identifying a preferred basis within it. For \(A=\operatorname{diag}(2,2,1)\), the two-dimensional leading right subspace has projector \(P=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,0)\). Rotating its two basis columns changes individual vectors but leaves \(VV^T=P\) unchanged. Compare projectors or principal angles rather than raw signed columns. Stability of the chosen subspace also needs a gap at its boundary; if truncation cuts through a repeated group, even that selected subspace may be nonunique.

For held-out PCA, fit the mean and feature directions on training data only. Transform validation/test rows using that same mean, and reconstruct with \(\hat x=\mu_{\mathrm{train}}+(x-\mu_{\mathrm{train}})V_kV_k^T\). Select rank using validation data, then report reconstruction on an untouched test set. Recomputing the test mean or test PCA changes the fitted procedure and leaks information into that evaluation.

**M7 · Stretch · mixed — Compare subspaces and evaluate PCA out of sample.** For diag(2,2,1), rotate the first two right singular vectors by 45°. What is the Frobenius distance between the old and new rank-two projectors? Is the rank-one optimum unique?

## 11. Three runnable coding labs

All three tasks use only the Python standard library, keep inputs unchanged, and reject booleans, non-finite values, or malformed shapes with ValueError. Matrices are lists of rows. Validation helpers are supplied in the browser; NumPy experiments below run locally.

### Lab A — a small paired-direction construction

Open [2×2 SVD](../../labs/exercises.py). Implement `svd_2x2(matrix)`, returning `(U, singular_values, Vt)` with 2×2 orthogonal factors and two nonnegative descending gains. Scale A by its largest absolute entry first; zero A may return identity factors and zero gains. For scaled A=[[a,b],[c,d]], form g₁₁=a²+c², g₁₂=ab+cd, g₂₂=b²+d². A top Gram eigenvector is (cos θ,sin θ), where θ=½atan2(2g₁₂,g₁₁−g₂₂); choose θ=0 when both arguments are zero. Its perpendicular completes V.

Compute the first gain as ‖Av₁‖ using the scaled matrix. Recover the second via |det(A)|/σ₁ in scaled units, which avoids subtracting nearly equal Gram eigenvalues. Normalize Av₁ for u₁; choose a perpendicular u₂ with the sign needed for the determinant. Restore gain units. Reject non-finite reported arithmetic. This construction is useful for small visual experiments, not a general stable SVD algorithm: scaling and the determinant shortcut do not guarantee relative accuracy in a tiny singular value or recover distinctions already rounded away. A computed zero is not a certificate of exact rank.

### Lab B — spend a rank budget

Open [rank truncation](../../labs/exercises.py). Implement `truncate_rank(left, singular_values, right_t, k)`. Inputs are reduced factors with shapes m×p, length p, and p×n, where p=min(m,n)≥1, and singular values are nonnegative and descending. The supplied `_validated_svd_factors` checks shapes, gains, and approximate orthonormality (absolute dot-product tolerance 10⁻⁹). Treat accepted factors as the supplied decomposition; no eigensolver is needed. Require integer k between 0 and p, excluding bools. Return the m×n sum of the first k outer products. Zero gains are valid, k=0 returns a zero matrix, and non-finite result arithmetic raises ValueError.

### Lab C — account for squared variation

Open [explained variance](../../labs/exercises.py). Implement `explained_variance(singular_values)`, returning `(ratios, cumulative)`, two lists of the same length. Require a nonempty finite nonnegative descending list. Scale by the largest gain before squaring to avoid avoidable overflow and underflow. All-zero input raises ValueError because the fractions are undefined. Repeated or trailing-zero gains are valid. Do not force the final value to one by overwriting a computed result; ordinary floating-point tolerance handles summation. Explain why dividing raw gains by their sum would answer the wrong question.

Run `python -m labs.checks svd-2x2`, `python -m labs.checks truncate-rank`, and `python -m labs.checks explained-variance`. Add `--reference` after an attempt to check the supplied implementations.

## 12. Exercises · by hand

**A1 · Foundation · paper — a missing input channel.** For A=[[3,0,0],[0,2,0]], give its singular values, rank, nullity, and minimum output length over all unit inputs.

**A2 · Core · paper — prove the paired directions.** Starting with an orthonormal eigenbasis of AᵀA, construct the positive-gain left singular vectors and prove their orthonormality. Explain what to do with zero gains.

**A3 · Foundation · paper — signs live in the factors.** Give one SVD of diag(−3,1), with descending nonnegative gains. State why negative eigenvalues do not force negative singular values.

**A4 · Core · paper — a rectangular shape audit.** A is 5×3 of rank two. Give full, reduced, and compact factor shapes, then the dimensions of its range, row space, null space, and left null space in that order.

**A5 · Core · paper — one step versus an invariant line.** For A=[[1,2],[0,1]], compute its eigenvalues, the length of Ae₂, and its singular values from the eigenvalues of AᵀA.

**A6 · Core · paper — two error budgets.** A matrix has singular values (5,3,1). Give its spectral norm, squared Frobenius norm, rank-one spectral error, and rank-one squared Frobenius error.

**A7 · Core · paper — optimal need not be unique.** For A=diag(3,1), compare B=diag(3,0) and C=diag(2,0). Give the spectral and squared Frobenius errors of each, and say which are optimal under each norm.

**A8 · Stretch · paper — prove an unavoidable lost direction.** Prove the spectral-norm rank-k approximation lower bound using a vector in span(v₁,…,vₖ₊₁) killed by any candidate B of rank at most k.

**A9 · Core · paper — minimum norm from positive channels.** For A=[[3,0,0],[0,2,0]] and b=(6,4), give all exact solutions and the minimum-norm solution. Prove the minimum claim with orthogonal coordinates.

**A10 · Foundation · paper — energy is squared.** For gains (6,3,1), give each explained-energy ratio, the fraction retained by two channels, and the remaining Frobenius error.

**A11 · Core · paper — center, score, reconstruct.** For X=[[8,1],[12,1],[10,0],[10,2]], compute the mean, top scores using v₁=(1,0), top explained-variance ratio, and best line's squared reconstruction error.

**A12 · Stretch · paper — the projection budget proof.** Prove the Frobenius rank-k approximation bound using the range projector of a candidate B. Justify why αᵢ=‖Puᵢ‖² lie in [0,1] and sum to rank(P).

## 13. Exercises · NumPy

Use float64 arrays and `np.linalg.svd`. It returns Vᵀ as its last factor for real input. Explicitly choose full or reduced factors, and record shapes. Do not compare vector signs against one reference.

**B1 · Foundation · NumPy — three reconstruction audits.** On [[1,2],[0,1]], [[3,0,0],[0,2,0]], and a 3×2 zero matrix, compute full and reduced SVDs. Check reconstruction and orthogonality using shape-appropriate identities. Explain which right null directions are absent from reduced factors.

**B2 · Core · NumPy — a tolerance changes a report.** For diag(1,10⁻⁸), count gains strictly above τσ₁ for τ=10⁻¹⁰,10⁻⁶, then repeat after multiplying A by 10⁶. Give the four numerical ranks and the exact rank. Explain the units benefit and remaining limitations of a relative threshold.

**B3 · Core · NumPy — see the Gram matrix forget.** For A=[[1,1],[0,ε]] with ε=10⁻⁴,10⁻⁸,10⁻¹⁰, compare direct SVD gains with square roots of Gram eigenvalues. Record any zero or negative computed Gram eigenvalue before applying a clipping policy. Explain why clipping does not recover the missing information.

**B4 · Core · NumPy — check the whole error curve.** For the 4×3 matrix [[3,0,0],[0,2,0],[0,0,1],[0,0,0]], compute A_k for k=0,1,2,3. Compare measured squared Frobenius errors and spectral errors with tail formulas, including the endpoints.

**B5 · Stretch · NumPy — a good compression can destroy the task.** Let A=diag(10,1) and all observed inputs equal e₂. Compute rank-one retained matrix energy, average squared output error, and relative output error. Compare with keeping the second channel instead. Which objective prefers which approximation?

**B6 · Core · NumPy — PCA reconstruction is affine.** For the dataset in A11, compute the centered SVD, scores, rank-one centered reconstruction, and reconstruction after restoring the mean. Give the ranks of the two reconstruction matrices and the squared residual. Explain why an affine line need not yield a rank-one uncentered data matrix.

## 14. Exercises · PyTorch

**C1 · Foundation · PyTorch — rectangular batches.** Stack a full-rank and a rank-one 3×2 matrix. Use float64 `torch.linalg.svd` with reduced factors. Reconstruct both with broadcasting or diagonal embedding, and audit factor shapes and paired equations. Explain why zero-gain columns must not be constructed by dividing by their gain.

**C2 · Core · PyTorch — repeated singular vectors can turn.** For A=2I₂, rotate U and V by the same angle while keeping Σ=2I₂. Verify that the reconstruction stays fixed. At rank one, compare the two retained projectors and their approximation errors; does equal optimal error identify one component?

**C3 · Core · PyTorch — whitening has a sample-size factor.** For the four-row dataset in A11, compute centered PCA scores and whiten both positive-variance directions using sample covariance divisor N−1. Verify WᵀW/(N−1)=I₂. Give the two whitening scale factors.

**C4 · Stretch · PyTorch — translate without changing variation.** Add (100,−50) to every row of the A11 dataset. Compare centered singular values and principal-subspace projectors before and after; compare uncentered singular values as well. Explain why signs of individual returned axes are the wrong invariant.

## 15. Derivations to own

1. Construct the full SVD from the spectral theorem, including all zero-gain and rectangular cases.
2. Recover the four subspaces and their orthogonal projectors from the full factors.
3. Derive spectral and Frobenius norm formulas, and the tail errors of a truncation.
4. Prove both rank-k approximation lower bounds, distinguishing existence from uniqueness.
5. Derive PCA's captured-variation/reconstruction equivalence and why an optimal affine subspace passes through the mean.
6. Derive the sample-covariance spectrum, explained-variance ratios, and the whitening identity with its divisor.

## 16. Exercises · cumulative

**M1 · Core · paper — a projector's SVD.** For the orthogonal projector P onto span((1,1)), give its singular values, spectral norm, squared Frobenius norm, and best rank-zero squared error. Why do eigenvalues and singular values coincide here?

**M2 · Core · paper — determinant forgets the shape.** For A=diag(4,1/4), give the product of singular values, determinant, largest gain, and smallest gain. Explain why unit area scaling does not imply length preservation.

**M3 · Core · paper — least squares with a left null direction.** For A=[[2,0],[0,1],[0,0]] and b=(4,3,5), use the singular channels to give the least-squares solution, residual b−Ax, squared error, and uniqueness verdict.

**M4 · Stretch · paper — a spectrum with no preferred axis.** For the centered rows (1,0),(−1,0),(0,1),(0,−1), compute the sample covariance and its eigenvalues. Show every line through the origin has the same squared reconstruction error and give that error.

**M5 · Core · paper — storage is a separate claim.** For a 100×80 matrix and k=5, compute dense storage, three-factor SVD storage, and two-factor storage after absorbing singular values. State what these counts do not establish about downstream prediction quality.

**M6 · Stretch · mixed — rank survives an invertible change, PCA need not.** Multiply the second feature of the A11 centered dataset by 3. Give its new descending singular values and leading feature axis. Compare its rank with the original, and explain why invertible feature scaling preserves rank but changes the PCA objective.

## 17. Exercises · checkpoint

**K1 · Foundation · gate — name both spaces.** For A=[[4,0,0],[0,1,0]], give singular values and bases for all four fundamental subspaces. State full factor shapes and explain why its smallest listed singular value is not its minimum amplification on unit inputs.

**K2 · Core · gate — justify universal existence.** Prove the SVD for an arbitrary real m×n matrix, including rank deficiency. Name the theorem that provides the right singular vectors and explain how the remaining left vectors are chosen.

**K3 · Core · gate — choose a defensible budget.** A matrix has gains (8,4,2,1). What smallest k retains at least 95% of squared energy? Give that truncation's spectral error, squared Frobenius error, and retained fraction. State the optimization claim those errors certify.

**K4 · Core · gate — rebuild the PCA calculation.** For X=[[8,1],[12,1],[10,0],[10,2]], give the mean, both sample covariance eigenvalues, the best affine line, and its squared reconstruction error. Give the error of the 45° line through the mean and explain the gap.

**K5 · Stretch · gate — audit three overclaims.** Refute each claim with a concrete example: positive listed singular values imply no null space; 99% retained matrix energy guarantees small relative output error on every input; an SVD always identifies unique signed principal directions.

**K6 · Stretch · gate — distinguish absence from smallness.** A centered dataset has N=4 rows and d=6 features. Give the largest possible rank and smallest possible feature-nullity. Explain how zero variance differs from tiny positive variance for explained-variance ratios, whitening, and numerical-rank reporting. Specify what happens to the ratios if every observation is identical.

## Mastery check

Given a rectangular matrix or a small dataset, identify the input and output spaces, reconstruct a map from paired directions, explain its null directions, choose and defend an approximation norm, and derive the corresponding error. For PCA, state the centering, feature scaling, covariance divisor, and reconstruction convention. A low-rank theorem is strongest when its scope is explicit.

**What to bring to Module 9:** singular values quantify both useful amplification and lost directions; a tiny positive value differs from an exact zero; forming a Gram matrix can hide that distinction; and a small residual under one metric need not answer the question your application asks.
