# Latent variables, the ELBO, and gradient estimators

Two problems block every modern generative model, and both are probability problems rather than engineering problems.

The first: a latent-variable model defines \(p_\theta(x)=\int p_\theta(x\mid z)p(z)\,dz\), and that integral is intractable. You cannot evaluate the likelihood you want to maximize.

The second: even once you have an objective of the form \(E_{q_\phi(z)}[f(z)]\), you need its gradient with respect to \(\phi\) — and \(\phi\) is inside the *distribution*, not just inside the function. The ordinary "differentiate under the integral" move needs care, and the two standard answers have wildly different variance.

This unit solves both. The evidence lower bound handles the first; the score-function and pathwise estimators handle the second. Between them they account for variational autoencoders, variational inference for Bayesian posteriors, the policy gradient in reinforcement learning, and the discrete-relaxation tricks used whenever a model must sample a token or route to an expert.

## 0. Prerequisite check

You need the change-of-variables machinery from [transformations, convolution, and Jacobians](03-transformations-convolution-jacobians.md), importance sampling and KL divergence from [Bayesian modeling and computation](09-bayesian-modeling-computation.md), and the fact that \(E[\nabla\log q]=0\), which appeared as the justification for policy-gradient baselines in [limit theorems and Monte Carlo](05-limit-theorems-monte-carlo.md).

### Learning route: one model, three approximation problems

Do not memorize “ELBO = reconstruction minus KL” as an isolated formula. Follow this chain:

1. The latent model defines \(p_\theta(x,z)\), but marginalization makes \(p_\theta(x)\) hard.
2. A variational distribution \(q_\phi(z\mid x)\) creates a computable lower bound whose gap is an explicit posterior KL.
3. Amortization replaces one optimization per observation with a learned inference map, adding another approximation gap.
4. Monte Carlo makes the bound usable in practice; score-function and pathwise gradients trade generality and variance differently.

At each step, label whether error comes from model misspecification, variational-family restriction, amortization, finite Monte Carlo, or optimization. “The ELBO is low” does not identify which one failed.

For multivariable differentiation, review the [local calculus bridge](03-transformations-convolution-jacobians.md#local-calculus-bridge-gradients-and-jacobians): gradient/Jacobian shapes, the chain rule, Hessians, and the separate conditions for differentiating an expectation.

## 1. The intractable marginal

A latent-variable model says: draw \(z\sim p(z)\) from a simple prior, then draw \(x\sim p_\theta(x\mid z)\). The observed likelihood requires marginalizing:

$$
p_\theta(x)=\int p_\theta(x\mid z)\,p(z)\,dz .
$$

For a linear-Gaussian decoder this integral is closed-form. For any neural decoder it is not, and the dimension of \(z\) makes quadrature hopeless.

**Why naive Monte Carlo fails.** The integral is an expectation, so sample it:

$$
\hat p_\theta(x)=\frac1K\sum_{k=1}^Kp_\theta(x\mid z_k),
\qquad z_k\sim p(z).
$$

This is unbiased, and it is useless. For a typical \(x\), almost all prior samples \(z_k\) produce a decoder that assigns \(x\) essentially zero probability; the estimator is dominated by the rare \(z\) near the true posterior \(p(z\mid x)\). The effective sample size collapses — exactly the proposal-mismatch failure diagnosed for importance sampling in the Bayesian-computation lesson. In \(d\) latent dimensions the mismatch grows geometrically.

The fix is to propose from something close to the posterior. That is what the next section builds.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Let \(z\in\{1,2\}\) with \(P(z=1)=0.3\), \(x\mid z=1\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) and \(x\mid z=2\sim\mathcal N(3,1)\). Write \(p(x)\) as a sum over \(z\) and evaluate \(p(x=0)\) to three decimals.
>
> **Hint:** \(p(0)=0.3\,\varphi(0)+0.7\,\varphi(-3)\) with \(\varphi(0)\approx0.3989\) and \(\varphi(3)\approx0.00443\); the answer is about 0.123.
>
> **Practice — Core:** For \(z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) and \(x\mid z\sim\mathcal N(z,0.01)\), compute the fraction of prior samples landing within two decoder standard deviations of \(x=3\), and say what that implies for \(K\).
>
> **Hint:** The relevant prior interval is [2.8,3.2]; compare its probability with 1/K.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** In the Core model with \(x=3\), write \(\hat p(x)=\frac1K\sum_k w_k\) with \(w_k=p(x\mid z_k)\), \(z_k\sim p(z)\), and show that \(\sum_k w_kz_k/\sum_k w_k\) instead estimates \(E[z\mid x=3]=300/101\). Then, with \(K=1000\), compute the expected number of draws in \([2.8,3.2]\) and the probability that none land there, and use this to explain why the fixed \(\operatorname{KL}(p(z\mid x)\Vert p(z))\approx6.22\) nats does not determine the realized effective sample size.
>
> **Hint:** Self-normalizing divides by \(\sum_k w_k\), whose expectation is \(K\,p(x)\), so the ratio targets a posterior mean; for the counts use \(1000\times0.00187\approx1.87\) and \((1-0.00187)^{1000}\approx0.15\).

## 2. The ELBO, derived twice

Introduce any distribution \(q(z)\) with support covering the posterior. Two derivations, and the second is the one worth memorizing.

**Derivation one — Jensen's inequality.**

$$
\log p_\theta(x)
=\log\int q(z)\frac{p_\theta(x,z)}{q(z)}dz
=\log E_q\!\left[\frac{p_\theta(x,z)}{q(z)}\right]
\;\ge\;
E_q\!\left[\log\frac{p_\theta(x,z)}{q(z)}\right]
=:\mathcal L(\theta,q).
$$

The inequality is Jensen applied to the concave \(\log\). This proves \(\mathcal L\) is a lower bound but says nothing about how loose it is.

**Derivation two — the exact decomposition.** Write \(p_\theta(x,z)=p_\theta(z\mid x)p_\theta(x)\) inside the bound:

$$
\mathcal L(\theta,q)
=E_q\!\left[\log\frac{p_\theta(z\mid x)p_\theta(x)}{q(z)}\right]
=\log p_\theta(x)-\operatorname{KL}\bigl(q(z)\,\Vert\,p_\theta(z\mid x)\bigr).
$$

Rearranged:

$$
\boxed{\;\log p_\theta(x)=\mathcal L(\theta,q)+\operatorname{KL}\bigl(q(z)\Vert p_\theta(z\mid x)\bigr)\;}
$$

**The gap is exactly a KL divergence.** Three consequences follow immediately, and they are the entire logic of variational inference:

1. The bound is tight precisely when \(q\) equals the true posterior.
2. Maximizing \(\mathcal L\) over \(q\) *is* minimizing \(\operatorname{KL}(q\Vert p(z\mid x))\) — you get posterior approximation for free while doing likelihood maximization.
3. Because \(\operatorname{KL}\ge0\), improving \(\mathcal L\) never overstates \(\log p_\theta(x)\). But a *higher ELBO* does not guarantee a higher likelihood, since the gap can shrink while the likelihood falls. Comparing models by ELBO compares bounds, not likelihoods.

The direction matters. This is the **reverse** KL \(\operatorname{KL}(q\Vert p)\), which is mode-seeking: it punishes \(q\) placing mass where \(p\) has none, and tolerates \(q\) ignoring entire modes of \(p\). Variational posteriors are therefore characteristically too narrow.

**The practical form.** Split the joint:

$$
\mathcal L=\underbrace{E_q\bigl[\log p_\theta(x\mid z)\bigr]}_{\text{reconstruction}}
-\underbrace{\operatorname{KL}\bigl(q(z)\Vert p(z)\bigr)}_{\text{stay near the prior}} .
$$

Every VAE loss you have read is this line with a sign flip.

## 3. Amortization

Optimizing a separate \(q\) per datapoint is expensive. Amortized inference trains one encoder \(q_\phi(z\mid x)\) to output variational parameters for any \(x\):

$$
\mathcal L(\theta,\phi)=E_{q_\phi(z\mid x)}\bigl[\log p_\theta(x\mid z)\bigr]-\operatorname{KL}\bigl(q_\phi(z\mid x)\Vert p(z)\bigr).
$$

This introduces a second gap. The total looseness is now

$$
\log p_\theta(x)-\mathcal L
=\underbrace{\operatorname{KL}(q^\star\Vert p(z\mid x))}_{\text{approximation gap}}
+\underbrace{\mathcal L(q^\star)-\mathcal L(q_\phi)}_{\text{amortization gap}},
$$

where \(q^\star\) is the best member of the variational family for this \(x\). The first is the price of the family (for example, diagonal Gaussians cannot represent correlated posteriors); the second is the price of using a shared network. They have different fixes — richer family versus more encoder capacity or per-datapoint refinement — so diagnose which one dominates before changing anything.

**The Gaussian KL, in closed form.** For \(q=\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) and \(p=\mathcal N(0,1)\),

$$
E_q[\log q]=-\tfrac12\log(2\pi\sigma^2)-\tfrac12,
\qquad
E_q[\log p]=-\tfrac12\log(2\pi)-\tfrac12(\sigma^2+\mu^2),
$$

so

$$
\operatorname{KL}\bigl(\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\Vert\mathcal N(0,1)\bigr)
=\tfrac12\bigl(\sigma^2+\mu^2-1-\log\sigma^2\bigr).
$$

For a diagonal Gaussian this sums over coordinates. The closed form matters: it removes one source of Monte Carlo noise entirely, which is why the KL term is almost never sampled in practice.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Evaluate the Gaussian KL at \(\mu=0,\sigma=1\) and confirm it is zero.
>

>

>

## 4. The gradient problem

Now the second obstacle. We need

$$
\nabla_\phi\,E_{q_\phi(z)}\bigl[f(z)\bigr]
=\nabla_\phi\int q_\phi(z)f(z)\,dz .
$$

The parameter sits in the measure. Moving the gradient inside gives \(\int\nabla_\phi q_\phi(z)\,f(z)\,dz\), which is **not** an expectation under \(q_\phi\) and so cannot be sampled directly. Two constructions repair this, and they are genuinely different — not two implementations of one idea.

### Estimator one: the score function (REINFORCE)

Use the log-derivative identity \(\nabla_\phi q_\phi=q_\phi\nabla_\phi\log q_\phi\):

$$
\nabla_\phi E_{q_\phi}[f(z)]
=\int q_\phi(z)f(z)\nabla_\phi\log q_\phi(z)\,dz
=E_{q_\phi}\bigl[f(z)\,\nabla_\phi\log q_\phi(z)\bigr].
$$

Now it *is* an expectation, so sample it. Properties:

- **Requires almost nothing.** \(f\) need not be differentiable, or even continuous. \(z\) may be discrete.
- **Unbiased**, given that differentiation and integration may be exchanged.
- **Admits baselines.** Since \(E_{q_\phi}[\nabla_\phi\log q_\phi]=\nabla_\phi\!\int q_\phi=\nabla_\phi1=0\), subtracting any constant \(b\) keeps the estimator unbiased: \(E[(f(z)-b)\nabla\log q_\phi]\). This is the identical argument that licenses advantage baselines in [policy gradients](../13-reinforcement-learning/02-policy-gradients-actor-critic.md).
- **High variance**, because \(f\) multiplies a score that can be large, and no information about \(f\)'s *shape* is used — only its value.

### Estimator two: the pathwise (reparameterization) gradient

Suppose \(z\) can be written as a deterministic, differentiable transform of parameter-free noise:

$$
z=g_\phi(\varepsilon),
\qquad
\varepsilon\sim p(\varepsilon)\ \text{independent of }\phi .
$$

Then the expectation is over a fixed distribution and the gradient passes straight through:

$$
\nabla_\phi E_{q_\phi}[f(z)]
=\nabla_\phi E_{p(\varepsilon)}\bigl[f(g_\phi(\varepsilon))\bigr]
=E_{p(\varepsilon)}\bigl[\nabla_zf(g_\phi(\varepsilon))\,\nabla_\phi g_\phi(\varepsilon)\bigr].
$$

For a Gaussian, \(z=\mu+\sigma\odot\varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\) — a location–scale transformation, which is exactly the change-of-variables construction of the transformations lesson. Properties: it needs \(f\) differentiable and \(g\) differentiable in \(\phi\); it fails outright for discrete \(z\); and it typically has **far** lower variance because it uses the gradient of \(f\), not just its value.

### How much lower? An exact comparison

Take \(q_\mu=\mathcal N(\mu,1)\) and \(f(z)=z\), so the true gradient is \(\nabla_\mu E[z]=1\).

*Score function.* \(\nabla_\mu\log q_\mu(z)=z-\mu\), so the single-sample estimator is \(z(z-\mu)\). Writing \(z=\mu+\varepsilon\):

$$
E\bigl[z(z-\mu)\bigr]=E[(\mu+\varepsilon)\varepsilon]=1,
$$

$$
E\bigl[z^2(z-\mu)^2\bigr]=E\bigl[(\mu+\varepsilon)^2\varepsilon^2\bigr]
=\mu^2E[\varepsilon^2]+2\mu E[\varepsilon^3]+E[\varepsilon^4]
=\mu^2+3,
$$

so the variance is \(\mu^2+3-1=\mu^2+2\).

*Pathwise.* \(z=\mu+\varepsilon\), so \(\nabla_\mu f(z)=1\) identically. The estimator is the constant \(1\): **variance zero**, exactly.

The contrast is stark and it is not an artifact of the toy problem: the score-function variance even *grows* with \(\mu\), meaning it degrades as the distribution moves away from the origin, while the pathwise estimator is exact. This is why continuous latent variables are reparameterized whenever possible, and why discrete latents are the hard case.

## 5. Discrete latents: Gumbel-max and its relaxation

When \(z\) is a category, no differentiable reparameterization exists — the map from parameters to a discrete sample is piecewise constant, so its derivative is zero almost everywhere and undefined on a measure-zero set. Two tools.

**The Gumbel-max trick.** Let \(G_1,\ldots,G_K\) be iid standard Gumbel, so \(G_i=-\log(-\log U_i)\) with \(U_i\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)\). Then

$$
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_i\bigl(\log\pi_i+G_i\bigr)\sim\mathrm{Categorical}(\pi).
$$

*Why.* \(P(\text{index }k\text{ wins})=\int f(g)\prod_{i\ne k}F\bigl(g+\log\pi_k-\log\pi_i\bigr)dg\) with \(F(g)=\exp(-e^{-g})\); the product of Gumbel CDFs is itself a Gumbel CDF with the log-weights accumulating inside the exponent, and the integral collapses to \(\pi_k/\sum_j\pi_j\).

Two properties worth noticing. The trick is **shift-invariant**: adding a constant to every \(\log\pi_i\) leaves the argmax unchanged, which is why unnormalized logits work directly. And taking the **top \(k\)** of \(\log\pi_i+G_i\) rather than the top 1 gives an exact sample of size \(k\) *without replacement* — the standard way to draw a diverse set of candidates in one pass.

**The Gumbel-softmax (Concrete) relaxation.** Replace the argmax with a temperature-controlled softmax:

$$
\tilde z=\operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{\log\pi+G}{\tau}\right).
$$

Now \(\tilde z\) is differentiable in \(\log\pi\), and as \(\tau\to0\) it converges to the one-hot sample. This buys pathwise gradients at the cost of **bias**: for \(\tau>0\) you are differentiating a different objective than the one you wrote down. The bias–variance tradeoff is explicit — small \(\tau\) means low bias and high gradient variance, large \(\tau\) the reverse — and \(\tau\) is typically annealed.

**Straight-through** takes the hard sample forward and the relaxed gradient backward. It is more biased still and has no guarantee behind it; treat it as a heuristic that often works, in the same spirit as the straight-through estimator for quantization in [constrained and composite optimization](../03-optimization/07-constrained-composite-distributed-optimization.md).

> **Practice — Foundation:** Draw a categorical sample from \(\pi=(0.2,0.5,0.3)\) using Gumbel-max with uniforms \(u=(0.8,0.5,0.3)\).

## 6. Tightening and reporting the bound

The single-sample ELBO is not the only bound. The importance-weighted bound

$$
\mathcal L_K=E\!\left[\log\frac1K\sum_{k=1}^K\frac{p_\theta(x,z_k)}{q_\phi(z_k\mid x)}\right],
\qquad z_k\stackrel{\text{iid}}\sim q_\phi ,
$$

satisfies \(\mathcal L_1\le\mathcal L_K\le\mathcal L_{K+1}\le\log p_\theta(x)\), when the importance weights and log expectations are well defined. Convergence \(\mathcal L_K\to\log p_\theta(x)\) needs conditions permitting convergence of the expected log estimate, such as positive weights bounded above and away from zero; a sample-mean law of large numbers alone is insufficient for that expectation claim. Inside the logarithm is an ordinary importance-sampling estimate of evidence, not a self-normalized estimate of a posterior expectation. Weight concentration still makes effective sample size a useful diagnostic, without certifying an accurate log-evidence estimate. The [IWAE paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1509.00519) develops the multi-sample bound. Reporting \(\mathcal L_{1}\) and \(\mathcal L_{64}\) together is a cheap, honest way to show how loose your bound is.

> **Practice — Foundation:** For \(z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\), \(x\mid z\sim\mathcal N(z,1)\), \(x=2\) and proposal \(q=\mathcal N(0,1)\), two draws \(z_1=0,z_2=1\) enter a \(K=2\) importance-weighted bound. Which distribution supplied them? Compute \(w_k=p(x,z_k)/q(z_k)\) and the realized \(\log\frac12(w_1+w_2)\).
>
> **Hint:** The draws come from the proposal \(q\) in the denominator; because \(q\) is the prior here, \(w_k=\varphi(2-z_k)\approx(0.0540,0.2420)\), giving about \(-1.911\).

## 7. Failure modes

- **Posterior collapse.** If the decoder is powerful enough to model \(x\) without \(z\), the optimizer drives \(q_\phi(z\mid x)\to p(z)\), the KL term to zero, and the latent becomes unused. Diagnose by reporting per-dimension KL, not the total.
- **Comparing ELBOs across models.** Different likelihood parameterizations (discretized versus continuous, different data scaling) change the number without changing the model's quality. Continuous densities are not probabilities and can be positive in log — the random-variables lesson's warning, resurfacing.
- **Reporting an ELBO as a likelihood.** It is a bound with an unmeasured gap. Report \(\mathcal L_K\) for growing \(K\) if you want to claim tightness.
- **KL annealing without disclosure.** Down-weighting the KL term optimizes a different objective; the resulting number is no longer a bound on \(\log p_\theta(x)\).
- **Using REINFORCE without a baseline** and concluding the method does not work.
- **Using a relaxation and reporting it as exact.** Gumbel-softmax gradients are biased at any \(\tau>0\).
- **Ignoring the amortization gap** and adding capacity to the wrong component.

### Worked example: an ELBO whose answer is known

Let \(z\sim N(0,1)\), \(x\mid z\sim N(z,1)\), and observe \(x=2\). Gaussian conditioning gives

$$
p(z\mid x=2)=N(1,1/2),
\qquad p(x)=N(0,2).
$$

For any Gaussian \(q(z)=N(m,v)\),

$$
\mathcal L(q)=\log p(x=2)-\operatorname{KL}\!\left(N(m,v)\Vert N(1,1/2)\right).
$$

Choosing the exact posterior makes the gap zero. Choosing the prior \(q=N(0,1)\) gives

$$
\operatorname{KL}\!\left(N(0,1)\Vert N(1,1/2)\right)
=\frac12\left[\log\frac{1/2}{1}+\frac{1+(0-1)^2}{1/2}-1\right]
\approx1.153.
$$

The generative model is unchanged; only inference is poor. This is why an ELBO gap cannot automatically be blamed on the decoder.

For \(z\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) and \(J=E[z^2]=\mu^2+\sigma^2\), reparameterize \(z=\mu+\sigma\varepsilon\). A one-sample pathwise gradient for \(\mu\) is \(2(\mu+\sigma\varepsilon)\), with expectation \(2\mu\). The score-function estimator \(z^2(z-\mu)/\sigma^2\) has the same expectation but usually much larger variance. This is the concrete reason to prefer reparameterization when available.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Two 4-dimensional VAEs report test-averaged per-dimension KL: run A \((0.002,0.001,0.003,0.002)\), run B \((3.1,0.002,2.4,0.001)\) nats. Compute each total KL, count active dimensions (KL above 0.01 nats), and say what run A's numbers suggest about \(q(z\mid x)\).
>

**K5 · Stretch · gate — Claim audit.** Is an importance-weighted evidence estimate a self-normalized posterior expectation?

**K6 · Stretch · gate — RE/RS transfer.** Compare a pathwise and score-function gradient implementation.

## Mastery check

Derive the ELBO both ways and state exactly what the gap is; produce the reconstruction-minus-KL form and the closed-form Gaussian KL from scratch; derive both gradient estimators, state the assumptions each requires, and reproduce the exact variance comparison; explain why discrete latents break reparameterization and what Gumbel-max and its relaxation do about it; and, shown a training run whose ELBO improves while samples worsen, name the term responsible and the diagnostic that proves it.

# Score matching, diffusion, and sampling from generative models

The previous unit handled an intractable *integral* — the marginal likelihood — with a bound. This unit handles an intractable *constant*, and then asks a question that is usually skipped entirely: once you have a trained generative model, what distribution are you actually sampling from?

The answer to the second question is almost never "the model's distribution", and the gap between the two is where a great deal of confused evaluation lives.

Three threads run through the unit. **Scores** let you learn a density without ever computing its normalizer. **Diffusion** turns score estimation into a noise-prediction regression, and turns out to be the evidence lower bound of the previous unit applied to a fixed hierarchical encoder. **Decoding** — temperature, top-\(k\), top-\(p\) — is distribution surgery performed after training, and it silently invalidates the likelihood numbers you reported.

## 0. Prerequisite check

You need the ELBO and the reparameterization trick from [latent variables and the ELBO](14-latent-variables-elbo-gradient-estimators.md), the convolution-of-Gaussians result from [transformations and convolution](03-transformations-convolution-jacobians.md), and the fact that a density is not a probability from [random variables and distributions](01-random-variables-distributions.md).

### Learning route: field, corruption, reversal, sampler

The chapter has four conceptual moves.

1. A score is a vector field \(\nabla_x\log p(x)\) that forgets the unknown normalizing constant.
2. Denoising replaces the unavailable data score with a supervised target under a known corruption process.
3. Diffusion repeats that corruption over noise levels, yielding closed-form forward marginals and a learned reverse process.
4. A numerical sampler, guidance rule, or decoding rule creates the distribution observed by users.

Always distinguish the data distribution, learned score model, ideal reverse-time distribution, and finite-step guided or truncated sampler. They coincide only under assumptions that should be stated.

## 1. The normalizer is the enemy; the score does not care

An energy-based model writes

$$
p_\theta(x)=\frac{\exp\bigl(-E_\theta(x)\bigr)}{Z_\theta},
\qquad
Z_\theta=\int\exp\bigl(-E_\theta(x)\bigr)dx .
$$

\(Z_\theta\) is an integral over the whole data space. In \(d=3\times10^5\) pixels it is not merely expensive, it is unapproachable. Maximum likelihood needs \(\nabla_\theta\log Z_\theta\), so maximum likelihood is blocked.

Now take the gradient **with respect to \(x\)** instead:

$$
s(x):=\nabla_x\log p_\theta(x)=-\nabla_xE_\theta(x)-\underbrace{\nabla_x\log Z_\theta}_{=0} .
$$

\(Z_\theta\) does not depend on \(x\), so it vanishes. The **score** \(\nabla_x\log p(x)\) is a complete description of the density up to a constant, and it is computable from an unnormalized model. This single observation is why the entire modern generative-modelling stack is built on scores rather than likelihoods.

Geometrically the score is a vector field pointing uphill in density: follow it and you move toward regions where data lives.

> **Practice — Foundation:** For \(p=\mathcal N(2,4)\), compute the score \(\nabla_x\log p(x)\) at \(x=0\) and at \(x=5\), and confirm that each points toward the mean 2.
>
> **Hint:** Differentiating \(-(x-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)\) gives \(-(x-2)/4\), so the values are \(+0.5\) and \(-0.75\).
>
> **Practice — Core:** Take \(E_1(x)=x^2/2\) and \(E_2(x)=x^2/2+7\). Compute both scores, both normalizers \(Z_1,Z_2\), and both normalized densities, and explain what this means for identifiability of \(E_\theta\).
>
> **Hint:** Both scores are \(-x\); \(Z_1=\sqrt{2\pi}\) and \(Z_2=e^{-7}\sqrt{2\pi}\), so the factor \(e^{-7}\) cancels and both densities are \(\mathcal N(0,1)\).
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** (a) For \(s(x)=x-x^3\) on \(\mathbb R\), recover \(\log p\) up to a constant and check normalizability. (b) Show \(s(x,y)=(-x-y,\;x-y)\) is not the score of any density. (c) Show \(s(x)=x\) integrates to a potential but is still not a valid score.
>
> **Hint:** Integrate along a path: (a) gives \(x^2/2-x^4/4\), whose exponential is integrable; in (b) the mixed partials are \(-1\) and \(+1\), so no potential exists; in (c) \(e^{x^2/2}\) has infinite integral.

## 2. Score matching and Hyvärinen's identity

We want \(s_\theta\approx\nabla_x\log p_{\text{data}}\), but we cannot evaluate the target — that is the whole problem. The Fisher divergence

$$
J(\theta)=\tfrac12E_{p_{\text{data}}}\Bigl[\bigl\lVert s_\theta(x)-\nabla_x\log p_{\text{data}}(x)\bigr\rVert^2\Bigr]
$$

still mentions the unknown. Expand the square:

$$
J(\theta)=E_p\Bigl[\tfrac12\lVert s_\theta\rVert^2\Bigr]
-E_p\bigl[s_\theta(x)^T\nabla_x\log p(x)\bigr]
+\text{const} .
$$

The middle term is the one to attack. Using \(p\nabla\log p=\nabla p\) and integrating by parts (the boundary term vanishes when \(p\) decays at infinity),

$$
-\int p(x)\,s_\theta(x)^T\nabla_x\log p(x)\,dx
=-\int s_\theta(x)^T\nabla_xp(x)\,dx
=\int p(x)\,\nabla_x\!\cdot s_\theta(x)\,dx .
$$

Therefore

$$
\boxed{\;J(\theta)=E_{p_{\text{data}}}\Bigl[\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\nabla_xs_\theta(x)\bigr)+\tfrac12\lVert s_\theta(x)\rVert^2\Bigr]+\text{const}\;}
$$

The unknown density appears only as the distribution we average over — which we have samples from. This is **Hyvärinen's identity**, and it is a genuinely surprising result: an objective that references an unknown function has been rewritten using only quantities we can compute.

The catch is \(\operatorname{tr}(\nabla_xs_\theta)\), the trace of a \(d\times d\) Jacobian, costing \(d\) backward passes. At \(d=10^5\) that is fatal. Sliced score matching estimates the trace with random projections (the Hutchinson estimator, \(\operatorname{tr}(A)=E_v[v^TAv]\) for \(E[vv^T]=I\)), which works but adds variance. The next section removes the problem entirely.

> **Practice — Foundation:** For \(s_\theta(x)=-\theta x\) in one dimension and data with \(E[x^2]=4\), write \(J(\theta)\) (up to its constant) using the identity and find the minimizing \(\theta\).
>
> **Hint:** The derivative of \(-\theta x\) is \(-\theta\), so \(J=-\theta+\tfrac12\theta^2E[x^2]=-\theta+2\theta^2\), minimized at \(\theta=0.25\), the score of \(\mathcal N(0,4)\).
>
> **Practice — Core:** Carry out the integration-by-parts step in one dimension, stating the decay condition used, then check it for \(p=\mathcal N(0,1)\) and \(s_\theta(x)=-\theta x\) by computing both \(-E_p[s_\theta(x)\,\partial_x\log p(x)]\) and \(E_p[s_\theta'(x)]\).
>
> **Hint:** The boundary term is \([s_\theta p]_{-\infty}^{\infty}=[-\theta x\varphi(x)]_{-\infty}^{\infty}=0\); both sides equal \(-\theta\) because \(E[x^2]=1\).
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\3&4\end{pmatrix}\), enumerate the four Rademacher vectors \(v\in\{\pm1\}^2\), confirm \(E_v[v^TAv]=\operatorname{tr}A=6\), compute the variance of the single-sample estimate, and prove that in general it equals \(\sum_{i<j}(A_{ij}+A_{ji})^2\).
>
> **Hint:** The values are \(10,2,2,10\), giving variance 16 \(=(1+3)^2\); in general \(v^TAv=\operatorname{tr}A+\sum_{i<j}(A_{ij}+A_{ji})v_iv_j\) and the products \(v_iv_j\) are uncorrelated with variance 1.

## 3. Denoising score matching: the trace disappears

Perturb the data with known noise. Let \(\tilde x=x+\sigma\varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\), giving the conditional

$$
q_\sigma(\tilde x\mid x)=\mathcal N(\tilde x;x,\sigma^2I),
\qquad
\nabla_{\tilde x}\log q_\sigma(\tilde x\mid x)=-\frac{\tilde x-x}{\sigma^2}=-\frac{\varepsilon}\sigma .
$$

The conditional score is available in closed form because we chose the noise. Vincent's identity states that matching this conditional score is equivalent, up to a constant, to matching the score of the *smoothed* marginal \(q_\sigma(\tilde x)=\int q_\sigma(\tilde x\mid x)p(x)dx\):

$$
E_{q_\sigma(\tilde x)}\Bigl[\bigl\lVert s_\theta(\tilde x)-\nabla\log q_\sigma(\tilde x)\bigr\rVert^2\Bigr]
=E_{p(x)q_\sigma(\tilde x\mid x)}\Bigl[\bigl\lVert s_\theta(\tilde x)-\nabla\log q_\sigma(\tilde x\mid x)\bigr\rVert^2\Bigr]+\text{const}.
$$

Substituting the conditional score and writing \(s_\theta(\tilde x)=-\hat\varepsilon_\theta(\tilde x)/\sigma\), the objective becomes

$$
E\Bigl[\bigl\lVert\hat\varepsilon_\theta(\tilde x)-\varepsilon\bigr\rVert^2\Bigr].
$$

**Predicting the noise is estimating the score.** That is the whole training objective of a diffusion model: add known noise, regress on it, and you have learned \(\nabla\log q_\sigma\) for free, with no trace, no normalizer, and no bound.

Two consequences worth stating plainly. The minimizer is \(\hat\varepsilon^\star(\tilde x)=E[\varepsilon\mid\tilde x]\), a conditional expectation — the same object that the law of total expectation in the joint-distributions lesson called the best mean-squared predictor. And you learn the score of the **smoothed** density \(q_\sigma\), not of \(p_{\text{data}}\); the two agree only as \(\sigma\to0\), which is precisely the regime where the score is hardest to estimate because data lies on a thin manifold. This tension is why a *range* of noise levels is used.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Verify \(\nabla_{\tilde x}\log\mathcal N(\tilde x;x,\sigma^2I)=-(\tilde x-x)/\sigma^2\), then evaluate it for \(x=1\), \(\sigma=0.5\), \(\tilde x=1.4\), and confirm it equals \(-\varepsilon/\sigma\) for the noise \(\varepsilon\) that produced \(\tilde x\).
>
> **Hint:** Differentiate \(-\lVert\tilde x-x\rVert^2/(2\sigma^2)\) in \(\tilde x\); here the score is \(-0.4/0.25=-1.6\) and \(\varepsilon=0.8\), so \(-\varepsilon/\sigma=-1.6\).
>
> **Practice — Core:** Show the minimizer of the denoising objective is \(E[\varepsilon\mid\tilde x]\) and rewrite it as a statement about \(E[x\mid\tilde x]\). Check both for \(x\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\), \(\sigma=1\): compute \(E[\varepsilon\mid\tilde x]\), \(E[x\mid\tilde x]\), and \(\nabla\log q_\sigma(\tilde x)\).
>
> **Hint:** Conditional expectation minimizes squared loss and \(\tilde x=E[x\mid\tilde x]+\sigma E[\varepsilon\mid\tilde x]\); here \(\tilde x\sim\mathcal N(0,2)\), both conditional means are \(\tilde x/2\), and the score \(-\tilde x/2\) equals \(-E[\varepsilon\mid\tilde x]/\sigma\).
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Data are \(\pm1\) with probability \(\tfrac12\) each, so \(\nabla\log q_\sigma(\tilde x)=(\tanh(\tilde x/\sigma^2)-\tilde x)/\sigma^2\). For \(\sigma=0.1\) and \(\sigma=2\), compute the variance of the regression target \(-\varepsilon/\sigma\) and the smoothed score at \(\tilde x=0.5\). Use the numbers to explain why small \(\sigma\) gives an accurate but poorly conditioned problem and large \(\sigma\) the reverse, and justify the weighting \(\lambda(\sigma)=\sigma^2\) across levels.
>
> **Hint:** Target variances are \(1/\sigma^2=100\) and \(0.25\); the scores are about \(+50\) (toward the datum 1) and \(-0.094\) (toward the blurred centre 0); weighting by \(\sigma^2\) turns each level's loss into \(E\lVert\sigma s_\theta+\varepsilon\rVert^2\), of order 1.

## 4. The forward process is a Gaussian chain with a closed form

Diffusion uses a whole schedule of noise levels, arranged as a Markov chain. With \(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_T\in(0,1)\),

$$
q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})=\mathcal N\bigl(\sqrt{1-\beta_t}\,x_{t-1},\;\beta_tI\bigr).
$$

Set \(\alpha_t=1-\beta_t\) and \(\bar\alpha_t=\prod_{s\le t}\alpha_s\). Composing Gaussians — the convolution result of the transformations lesson, since a scaled Gaussian plus an independent Gaussian is Gaussian with added variances — gives the **closed-form marginal**

$$
q(x_t\mid x_0)=\mathcal N\bigl(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0,\;(1-\bar\alpha_t)I\bigr),
\qquad
x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\varepsilon .
$$

**Check the induction once.** If \(x_{t-1}=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,\varepsilon'\), then

$$
x_t=\sqrt{\alpha_t}x_{t-1}+\sqrt{\beta_t}\,\varepsilon''
=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\sqrt{\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}\,\varepsilon'+\sqrt{1-\alpha_t}\,\varepsilon'' ,
$$

and the two independent Gaussian terms have total variance \(\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})+(1-\alpha_t)=1-\bar\alpha_t\). The schedule is called **variance-preserving** exactly because signal coefficient squared plus noise variance is \(\bar\alpha_t+(1-\bar\alpha_t)=1\).

This closed form is what makes training cheap: to train at step \(t\) you never simulate the chain, you jump straight to \(x_t\) in one draw.

**The reverse posterior is also exactly Gaussian** when conditioned on \(x_0\):

$$
q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)=\mathcal N(\tilde\mu_t,\tilde\beta_tI),
$$

$$
\tilde\mu_t=\frac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,\beta_t}{1-\bar\alpha_t}x_0
+\frac{\sqrt{\alpha_t}\,(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}{1-\bar\alpha_t}x_t,
\qquad
\tilde\beta_t=\frac{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}{1-\bar\alpha_t}\beta_t .
$$

The model does not know \(x_0\) at sampling time, so it predicts it (equivalently, predicts \(\varepsilon\)) and substitutes.

![Diffusion adds Gaussian noise forward with a closed-form marginal and learns to reverse it, while decoding truncates and renormalizes a trained distribution.](../assets/diffusion-and-decoding.svg)

> **Practice — Foundation:** For \(\beta=(0.5,0.5)\), compute \(\bar\alpha_1,\bar\alpha_2\) and the signal and noise coefficients at each step.
>
> **Hint:** Each alpha is one minus beta; cumulative alphas multiply.
>
> **Practice — Core:** Complete the induction above, stating where independence of \(\varepsilon'\) and \(\varepsilon''\) is used, and check the variance identity numerically for \(\beta=(0.5,0.5)\) at \(t=2\).
>
> **Hint:** Independent Gaussian noises add their scaled variances; here \(\alpha_2(1-\bar\alpha_1)+(1-\alpha_2)=0.25+0.5=0.75=1-\bar\alpha_2\).
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Show \(\tilde\beta_t\le\beta_t\) in general and compute \(\tilde\beta_2\) for \(\beta=(0.1,0.2)\). Then, for data \(x_0\sim\mathcal N(0,s^2)\), compute \(\operatorname{Var}(x_1\mid x_2)\), which does not condition on \(x_0\), for \(s^2=1\) and \(s^2=100\), and use the results to explain why \(\tilde\beta_t\le\beta_t\) does not bound the variance of the reverse law conditioned only on \(x_t\).
>
> **Hint:** \(\tilde\beta_2=(0.1/0.28)(0.2)\approx0.071\); with \(\operatorname{Var}x_1=0.9s^2+0.1\), \(\operatorname{Var}x_2=0.72s^2+0.28\), \(\operatorname{Cov}=\sqrt{0.8}\operatorname{Var}x_1\), you get 0.2 and about 0.249, the latter above \(\beta_2\).

## 5. Diffusion is the ELBO of a fixed-encoder hierarchical VAE

Put the previous unit next to section 4. A diffusion model is a latent-variable model with latents \(z=(x_1,\ldots,x_T)\), an encoder \(q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)\) that is **fixed, not learned**, and a decoder \(p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)\). Its ELBO is

$$
\log p_\theta(x_0)\ \ge\
E_q\Bigl[\log p(x_T)+\sum_t\log\frac{p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)}{q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})}\Bigr],
$$

which regroups into a sum of KL divergences between Gaussians — one per timestep — plus a reconstruction term. Because both distributions in each KL are Gaussian with known variances, each term reduces to a squared difference of means, and with the \(\varepsilon\)-parameterization and a particular weighting it collapses to

$$
E_{t,x_0,\varepsilon}\Bigl[\bigl\lVert\hat\varepsilon_\theta(x_t,t)-\varepsilon\bigr\rVert^2\Bigr] .
$$

The same objective arrived at from denoising score matching in section 3. **Two independent derivations, one loss.** That is the strongest evidence that the object is natural rather than engineered.

One honest caveat: the simple unweighted MSE used in practice is *not* the ELBO — it drops the per-timestep weights. It works better empirically, and it means the reported loss is not a likelihood bound. If you want a likelihood number, compute the weighted bound.

> **Practice — Foundation:** For \(T=2\) and \(\beta=(0.1,0.2)\), write the diffusion encoder \(q(x_1,x_2\mid x_0)\) as a product of two Gaussians with explicit means and variances, and state which of its parameters are learned.
>
> **Hint:** The forward chain is the encoder: \(q(x_1\mid x_0)=\mathcal N(\sqrt{0.9}\,x_0,0.1)\) and \(q(x_2\mid x_1)=\mathcal N(\sqrt{0.8}\,x_1,0.2)\), with nothing learned.
>

> **Practice — Core:** Two models have per-timestep noise-prediction MSEs \((0.10,0.50)\) (model A) and \((0.30,0.20)\) (model B) on a two-step schedule. Rank them under the unweighted sum and under weights \((5,1)\), and explain what this shows about changing the weighting.
>
> **Hint:** Unweighted totals are 0.6 and 0.5 (B wins); weighted totals are 1.0 and 1.7 (A wins), so the weights define which model the objective prefers.
>

> **Practice — Stretch:** Suppose the ELBO's timestep weights for the Core schedule are \((w,1)\) and all other bound terms are equal for A and B. For which \(w\) does B's lower unweighted loss coincide with a higher ELBO? Explain why an unweighted improvement therefore does not certify a likelihood improvement.
>
> **Hint:** B has the smaller weighted loss iff \(0.3w+0.2<0.1w+0.5\), that is \(w<1.5\); the unweighted loss certifies nothing about the bound unless the true weights are known to fall in that range.

## 6. Sampling: stochastic, deterministic, and guided

Training gives a score field. Getting samples is a separate algorithmic question.

- **Ancestral (stochastic) sampling** walks the reverse chain, adding fresh noise at each step. Many steps, high diversity.
- **Probability-flow ODE.** There is a deterministic ODE whose marginals match the stochastic process at every \(t\). Solving it gives sampling with far fewer steps, exactly invertible trajectories, and — because it is a deterministic change of variables — an exact likelihood via the change-of-variables formula of the transformations lesson. Determinism costs diversity at a fixed seed.
- **Classifier-free guidance** interpolates conditional and unconditional scores:

$$
\tilde s=s_\theta(x\mid\varnothing)+w\bigl(s_\theta(x\mid c)-s_\theta(x\mid\varnothing)\bigr).
$$

For \(w>1\) this is a score of \(p(x)\,p(c\mid x)^{w}\) up to normalization — a **sharpened**, temperature-like distribution, not \(p(x\mid c)\). Samples look better on human preference and are *less diverse and less faithful to the model's actual conditional*. Report \(w\); a guided FID is not comparable to an unguided one.

> **Practice — Foundation:** The forward SDE is \(dx=-\tfrac12x\,dt+dW\) on \(t\in[0,1]\). Write one Euler–Maruyama step of the reverse SDE \(dx=[-\tfrac12x-s(x,t)]dt+d\bar W\) run from \(t=1\) to \(t=0\) with \(N=10\) steps, stating the step size, the noise standard deviation per step, and the initialization.
>
> **Hint:** Stepping backward by \(\Delta=0.1\) gives \(x_{t-\Delta}=x_t+(\tfrac12x_t+s(x_t,t))\Delta+\sqrt{\Delta}\,z\) with noise sd \(\sqrt{0.1}\approx0.316\), started from the terminal law (approximately \(\mathcal N(0,1)\)).
>

> **Practice — Core:** For data \(\mathcal N(0,4)\) under the Foundation SDE, the exact marginal is \(\mathcal N(0,v_t)\) with \(v_t=4e^{-t}+1-e^{-t}\), so \(s(x,t)=-x/v_t\). Design a test that runs the reverse Euler–Maruyama sampler from \(\mathcal N(0,v_1)\) with \(N\in\{10,100,1000\}\) and checks the final variance against 4; predict how the error should scale with \(N\).
>
> **Hint:** The update is linear, so the variance obeys \(V\leftarrow(1+(\tfrac12-1/v_t)\Delta)^2V+\Delta\) exactly; it gives about 3.901, 3.990, 3.999, an error shrinking like \(1/N\).
>

> **Practice — Stretch:** Let \(p(x)=\mathcal N(0,1)\) and \(p(c\mid x)\propto\exp(-(x-2)^2/2)\). Compute \(p(x\mid c)\) and the distribution \(\propto p(x)p(c\mid x)^w\) targeted by guidance weight \(w=3\), and explain why guidance changes the sampling target even when every score is exact.
>
> **Hint:** Precisions add: \(p(x\mid c)=\mathcal N(1,\tfrac12)\), while \(w=3\) gives precision 4 and mean \(2w/(1+w)=1.5\), i.e. \(\mathcal N(1.5,0.25)\); the guided score is the exact score of a different, sharper law.

## 7. Decoding is distribution surgery

Autoregressive models raise the same issue in a form people rarely name. A trained language model defines \(p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t})\). Generation almost never samples from it.

**Temperature.** With logits \(z\),

$$
p_T(i)=\frac{\exp(z_i/T)}{\sum_j\exp(z_j/T)}\ \propto\ p(i)^{1/T} .
$$

\(T\to0\) concentrates on the argmax; \(T\to\infty\) tends to uniform; \(T=1\) is the model. Entropy increases monotonically in \(T\). This is the same exponential tilt that appeared as the maximum-entropy solution in [convexity and duality](../03-optimization/03-convexity-smoothness-duality.md) — temperature is the Lagrange multiplier.

**Top-\(k\) and top-\(p\) (nucleus).** Sort descending, keep either the top \(k\) tokens or the smallest prefix whose cumulative probability reaches \(p\), zero the rest, renormalize. This is conditioning on the event "the token is in the kept set" — a genuinely different distribution, with all tail mass redistributed onto the head.

**The consequence people skip.** Perplexity, cross-entropy, and every likelihood-based evaluation describe \(p_\theta\). Generation uses \(p_{T,k,p}\). These are different distributions, so:

- A perplexity improvement need not improve generations at your decoding settings.
- Two systems compared at different temperatures are not comparable.
- Likelihood-based detection, watermarking, and calibration arguments all assume the untruncated distribution.
- Truncation removes exactly the tail where rare-but-correct tokens live, which is why factual recall and greedy decoding interact badly.

Always report decoding parameters alongside any generation result. A generation claim without \(T\), \(k\), \(p\), and the seed policy is not reproducible.

**Sampling without replacement.** To draw \(k\) distinct candidates in one pass, take the \(k\) largest of \(\log p_i+G_i\) with Gumbel noise — the Gumbel top-\(k\) trick from the previous unit. This is exactly a without-replacement sample, unlike \(k\) independent draws.

> **Practice — Foundation:** For logits \((0,\log 3)\), compute the distribution at \(T=1\) and at \(T=2\).
>
> **Hint:** At T=1 normalize (1,3); at T=2 normalize (1,sqrt(3)).
>
> **Practice — Core:** Show \(p_T\propto p^{1/T}\) follows from the softmax definition, check it for logits \((2,1,0)\) at \(T=0.5\) by computing \(p_T\) both from the logits and by squaring and renormalizing \(p_1\), and explain why adding a constant to all logits changes nothing.
>
> **Hint:** \(e^{z_i/T}=(e^{z_i})^{1/T}\); both routes give about \((0.867,0.117,0.016)\), and a shift \(c\) multiplies every term by \(e^{c/T}\), which cancels.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** A model's distribution over four candidate answers is \((0.55,0.25,0.12,0.08)\), and the correct answer is the fourth. Compute the nucleus set at \(p=0.9\), the probability of a correct generation before and after truncation, and propose an evaluation protocol that would have detected the problem.
>
> **Hint:** Cumulative mass is 0.55, 0.80, 0.92, so three answers survive and the correct one drops from 0.08 to 0; evaluate accuracy or coverage at the deployed decoding settings, not only likelihood.

## 8. Failure modes

- **Reporting the simple diffusion MSE as a likelihood bound.** It is the unweighted loss; the ELBO has weights.
- **Comparing guided and unguided samples** on the same metric without saying so.
- **Reporting generation quality without decoding parameters.**
- **Assuming perplexity predicts sample quality** across decoding settings.
- **Score matching at a single small \(\sigma\)**, which estimates the score accurately only where there is data — nowhere useful at initialization.
- **Forgetting that the learned score belongs to the smoothed density**, not the data density.
- **Treating the probability-flow likelihood as the stochastic sampler's likelihood.** They are different samplers.
- **Using a relaxation or a truncation and calling the result a sample from the model.** It is a sample from a modified model; name it.

### Worked example: follow one datum through noise and back

Take \(x_0=2\), \(\beta_1=0.1\), and \(\beta_2=0.2\). Then \(\alpha=(0.9,0.8)\) and \(\bar\alpha_2=0.72\), so

$$
x_2=\sqrt{0.72}\,x_0+\sqrt{0.28}\,\varepsilon.
$$

Conditional on \(x_0=2\), this is \(N(2\sqrt{0.72},0.28)\), with mean about 1.697 and standard deviation about 0.529. If \(x_2=1.5\), the noise that produced it was

$$
\varepsilon=\frac{1.5-2\sqrt{0.72}}{\sqrt{0.28}}\approx-0.372.
$$

If a network predicts \(\hat\varepsilon=-0.30\), its implied clean prediction is

$$
\hat x_0
=\frac{x_2-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_2}\,\hat\varepsilon}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_2}}
\approx1.955.
$$

This connects the training label, noise-prediction loss, and clean-data parameterization. It is not yet a sample from the data distribution: generation must start from the terminal noise law and apply every reverse transition or a justified numerical approximation. Guidance changes those reverse scores again, so sample quality is a property of the model–sampler pair, not of the likelihood model alone.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Model A has denoising loss 0.051 and model B 0.049. With a 10-step solver A scores FID 12.0 and B 15.0; with 1000 steps A scores 4.1 and B 3.8. Which model is better under each solver, and does a lower training loss guarantee better samples under every solver?
>
> **Hint:** B wins at 1000 steps but loses at 10; sample quality mixes score-approximation error with solver and initialization error, so the loss alone guarantees nothing.
>

> **Practice — Core:** One noising step from \(x_0=0\) with \(\beta=0.04\) should give \(x_1\sim\mathcal N(0,0.04)\). A buggy implementation multiplies the noise by \(\beta\) instead of \(\sqrt\beta\). Describe a test (\(10^5\) draws, seed 0) that detects the bug, and state the empirical variance each version should produce.
>
> **Hint:** The correct step has variance \(\beta=0.04\) (sd 0.2); the bug gives \(\beta^2=0.0016\), a 25-fold gap far beyond the Monte Carlo error of about \(0.04\sqrt{2/10^5}\).
>

> **Practice — Stretch:** With a fixed trained score model, design an ablation over guidance \(w\in\{1,2,3\}\) and step counts \(N\in\{10,50,250,1000\}\) (5 seeds, \(10^4\) samples per cell) that separates guidance effects from discretization error, stating exactly which differences estimate each.
>
> **Hint:** At fixed \(w\), metric\((N)-\)metric\((1000)\) estimates discretization error; at \(N=1000\), differences across \(w\) estimate the guidance effect; the seed spread gives their standard errors.

## 9. Runnable labs

**Lab A — decoding as distribution surgery.** Implement `decode_distribution` in the [learner exercises file](../../labs/exercises.py). Given logits, a temperature, and a nucleus threshold, divide the logits by the temperature, convert to probabilities with a numerically stable softmax, keep the smallest prefix of the descending-sorted probabilities whose cumulative mass reaches the threshold, and renormalize over the kept tokens, returning probabilities in the original index order. Break ties toward the lower index. Reject empty logits, non-finite values, non-positive temperature, and a threshold outside \((0,1]\).

Then investigate: sweep \(T\) from \(0.1\) to \(5\) on a fixed logit vector and plot the entropy. Sweep the nucleus threshold and record how many tokens survive. Then construct a distribution where the correct token sits just outside the nucleus, and quantify how the probability of a correct generation changes.

**Lab B — the forward diffusion schedule.** Implement `forward_diffusion_coefficients` in the [learner exercises file](../../labs/exercises.py). Given a list of \(\beta_t\in(0,1)\), return for each timestep the triple \((\bar\alpha_t,\;\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t},\;\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t})\). Reject an empty schedule and any \(\beta\) outside \((0,1)\).

Then investigate: compare a linear and a cosine schedule at \(T=1000\) by plotting \(\bar\alpha_t\). Verify numerically that composing the per-step Gaussians matches the closed-form marginal by simulating the chain and comparing sample moments. Then compute \(\tilde\beta_t\) and confirm \(\tilde\beta_t\le\beta_t\).

## 10. Derivations to own

1. Why \(\nabla_x\log p_\theta(x)\) is free of \(Z_\theta\).
2. Hyvärinen's identity, including the integration-by-parts step and its decay condition.
3. The conditional score \(-(\tilde x-x)/\sigma^2\) and the reduction of denoising score matching to noise prediction.
4. That the minimizer of the denoising objective is \(E[\varepsilon\mid\tilde x]\).
5. The closed-form marginal \(q(x_t\mid x_0)\) by induction, and why the schedule is variance-preserving.
6. The reverse posterior mean \(\tilde\mu_t\) and variance \(\tilde\beta_t\).
7. \(p_T\propto p^{1/T}\), and top-\(p\) as conditioning on a set.

## Prediction experiment

Predict both the baseline and failure-preset results before revealing the calculation. Record the assumptions, change one control at a time, and explain the boundary case. This small deterministic model isolates a mechanism; it is not an empirical validation of a trained system.

```lab
lab: ps-score
```

## 11. End-of-unit practice (graded)

Work each problem before opening its authored solution. Written proofs and design answers require self-review against the rubric; numeric fields check only the stated quantities.


**Foundation**

**A1 · Foundation · paper — Cumulative problem 1.** Compute the score of \(\mathcal N(3,4)\) at \(x=1\).

**A2 · Foundation · paper — Cumulative problem 2.** For \(\beta=(0.1,0.2)\), compute \(\bar\alpha_1,\bar\alpha_2\) and the noise coefficient at \(t=2\).

**A3 · Foundation · paper — Cumulative problem 3.** For logits \((2,1,0)\), give the distribution at \(T=1\) and the surviving set at \(p=0.7\).

**Core**

**A4 · Core · paper — Cumulative problem 4.** Derive Hyvärinen's identity in one dimension and state precisely which boundary condition you used.

**A5 · Core · paper — Cumulative problem 5.** Show that predicting \(\varepsilon\) and predicting \(x_0\) are equivalent parameterizations, and write the conversion formula.

**A6 · Core · paper — Cumulative problem 6.** Let \(p(x)=\mathcal N(0,1)\) and \(p(c\mid x)\propto\exp(-(x-1)^2/2)\). Compute \(p(x\mid c)\), show that classifier-free guidance with exact scores and \(w=3\) targets a density \(\propto p(x)p(c\mid x)^3\) rather than \(p(x\mid c)\), and give the mean and variance of that target.

**A7 · Core · paper — Cumulative problem 7.** A model's perplexity improves by 4% but human raters prefer the old model's generations at \(T=0.8,p=0.95\). Give three explanations consistent with both facts.

**Stretch**

**A8 · Stretch · paper — Cumulative problem 8.** Prove that the probability-flow ODE permits exact likelihood computation, naming the theorem from the transformations lesson that makes it possible, and state the cost.

**A9 · Stretch · paper — Cumulative problem 9.** A team reports, for guidance weights \(w=1,3,5,7\), FID \(18.0,11.5,9.2,8.4\), precision \(0.61,0.74,0.81,0.85\) and recall \(0.63,0.52,0.41,0.30\), and concludes the model has improved. Critique the claim, compute the relative drop in recall from \(w=1\) to \(w=7\), name the quantity that is silently degrading, and design the measurement that exposes it.

**A10 · Stretch · paper — Cumulative problem 10.** Data are \(x=\pm1\) with probability \(\tfrac12\) each, and denoising score matching is run at a single fixed \(\sigma=0.5\) with infinite data and capacity. Argue whether it recovers the data score, write the function it does recover, and compute the variance of the distribution an exact sampler with that score produces, compared with the data variance.


## Six-part checkpoint

Complete these without notes, then use the solutions to audit assumptions and reasoning. Passing a numeric check alone does not establish mastery. For implementation and transfer, retain the code/results or written protocol as evidence.

**K1 · Foundation · gate — Concept.** What is a score function in score-based modeling?

**K2 · Core · gate — Derivation.** Derive the score of a one-dimensional Gaussian with mean mu and variance v.

**K3 · Core · gate — Calculation.** Find the score of N(0,4) at x=2.

**K4 · Core · gate — Implementation audit.** Reproduce two settings of the ps-score experiment independently, including its failure preset. State a numerical invariant or analytic oracle and explain what the plot does not establish.

**K5 · Stretch · gate — Claim audit.** Does an exact continuous-time score make every discretized sampler exact?

**K6 · Stretch · gate — RE/RS transfer.** Validate a diffusion sampler before a large model run.

## Mastery check

Explain why the score sidesteps the normalizer; derive Hyvärinen's identity and say why its trace term is impractical; derive denoising score matching and show it is noise prediction; derive the closed-form diffusion marginal and the reverse posterior; explain in one paragraph why the diffusion loss is simultaneously an ELBO and a score-matching objective; and, given a generation result, state exactly which distribution it was sampled from and what that does to the reported likelihood numbers.

---

title: Observational causal inference, quasi-experiments, and missing data
prerequisites: [math.statistics.exponential-families-regression-glms, math.statistics.sampling-design-ml-evaluation]

# Observational causal inference, quasi-experiments, and missing data

A randomized experiment answers a causal question by construction. Most of the data you will actually analyze was not randomized: production logs, user telemetry, historical evaluation runs, scraped corpora, human ratings collected whenever a rater happened to be available. The question you care about is still causal — *would accuracy improve if we changed the system?* — but the data was generated by a process that mixed the intervention with everything correlated with it.

This unit develops the machinery for that situation. The central discipline is a separation that no amount of estimation skill can substitute for: **identification** asks whether the causal quantity is a function of the observable distribution at all, and **estimation** asks how well you can approximate that function from a finite sample. Every technique below — graphs, backdoor adjustment, propensity weighting, doubly robust estimation, instruments, difference-in-differences — is an identification argument first and a statistical procedure second.

The unit ends with missing data, which is not an appendix. The fundamental problem of causal inference *is* a missing-data problem: for every unit you observe one potential outcome and the other is missing, and the mechanism that decided which one you see is the treatment assignment. The MCAR/MAR/MNAR taxonomy and the ignorability conditions of causal inference are the same mathematics wearing different notation.

By the end, you should be able to state a causal estimand precisely; encode assumptions in a DAG and read conditional independences off it by d-separation; apply the backdoor criterion and know when adjustment *creates* bias instead of removing it; derive standardization, inverse probability weighting, and the doubly robust estimator, and prove what each one needs; diagnose positivity failures; use instruments, difference-in-differences, and regression discontinuity, along with the assumption each one trades for; quantify sensitivity to unmeasured confounding; classify missingness as MCAR, MAR, or MNAR; and choose between complete cases, single imputation, and multiple imputation with Rubin's rules.

## Learning route: identification before estimation

Use four passes rather than reading the methods as a menu.

1. **Define the counterfactual contrast.** Name treatment versions, population, time horizon, and whether the target is ATE, ATT, or CATE.
2. **Argue identification.** Draw assignment and measurement, then state the exchangeability, consistency, positivity, exclusion, or trend assumption that turns the counterfactual into observed-data quantities.
3. **Estimate and diagnose.** Only now choose standardization, weighting, AIPW, IV, DiD, RD, or imputation. Check overlap, balance, nuisance fit, and dependence at the units relevant to the claim.
4. **Stress the untestable assumption.** Use negative controls, falsification tests, and sensitivity parameters. Sampling error around a nonidentified target is false precision.

For every problem, write an identification line before any estimator: \(\text{causal estimand}=\text{observed-data functional}\) under named assumptions.

## 0. A regression coefficient is not an effect

Lesson 11 established that a regression coefficient is a conditional comparison: with the other columns of the design matrix held fixed, \(\beta_j\) is the difference in fitted conditional mean per unit of \(x_j\). Nothing in that derivation licenses the sentence "raising \(x_j\) would raise \(Y\) by \(\beta_j\)."

The gap has a precise shape. A coefficient describes

$$
E[Y\mid X_j=x+1,X_{-j}]-E[Y\mid X_j=x,X_{-j}],
$$

a contrast between two subpopulations that *already differ* in \(X_j\). A causal claim describes

$$
E[Y\mid \operatorname{do}(X_j=x+1)]-E[Y\mid \operatorname{do}(X_j=x)],
$$

a contrast between two states of the same population under two interventions. Conditioning selects units; intervening changes them. The two coincide only under assumptions that the regression itself cannot check, because both quantities are computed from data that looks identical.

**Worked example — the retrieval-augmented system that appears to hurt.** You log 200,000 production requests. Some were served by a retrieval-augmented pipeline, some by the base model, with routing decided by a heuristic that sends hard queries to retrieval. Regressing answer quality on a retrieval indicator gives a negative coefficient. The coefficient is a correct description of the log: retrieval-served answers *were* worse. It is a useless answer to "should we route everything to retrieval," because query difficulty caused both the routing and the quality. No standard error, robustness check, or larger sample repairs this. The defect is in identification, and a tighter confidence interval only makes the wrong number look more credible.

> **Practice — Foundation:** In the routing log, mean quality is 0.67 for retrieval-served queries and 0.82 for base-model queries. Say whether the difference \(-0.15\) estimates \(E[Y\mid T=1]-E[Y\mid T=0]\) or \(E[Y\mid\operatorname{do}(T=1)]-E[Y\mid\operatorname{do}(T=0)]\), and state in one sentence the difference between conditioning on \(T=t\) and intervening to set \(T=t\).
>
> **Hint:** A log difference is always the conditional contrast between groups that were routed differently (and so differ in difficulty); an intervention sets \(T\) for the same population.
>
> **Practice — Core:** Queries are easy or hard with probability \(\tfrac12\) each; retrieval is used with probability 0.2 on easy and 0.8 on hard queries. Mean quality is 0.95 (retrieval) and 0.90 (base) on easy queries, and 0.60 and 0.50 on hard ones. Compute the coefficient from regressing quality on the retrieval indicator alone, and the effect of routing everything to retrieval, and say which sentence each number supports.
>
> **Hint:** Treated queries are 20% easy, so \(E[Y\mid T=1]=0.2(0.95)+0.8(0.60)=0.67\) and \(E[Y\mid T=0]=0.82\), giving \(-0.15\); the intervention averages the stratum effects \(0.05\) and \(0.10\) over the 50/50 mix, giving \(+0.075\).
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Let \(U\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(1/2)\), \(X=U\), and the structural equation \(Y=3U-X\). Compute the population regression slope of \(Y\) on \(X\), then the change in each unit's \(Y\) under \(\operatorname{do}(X=x+1)\), and identify the structural feature that makes the signs disagree.
>
> **Hint:** Observed \(Y=2U=2X\), so the slope is \(+2\), while the structural coefficient on \(X\) is \(-1\) for every unit; \(U\) is a common cause of \(X\) and \(Y\), and no sample size changes that.

## 1. Potential outcomes and the estimand you actually want

Fix a binary treatment \(T\in\{0,1\}\). For each unit \(i\), postulate two **potential outcomes**: \(Y_i(1)\), the outcome if treated, and \(Y_i(0)\), the outcome if untreated. Both are properties of the unit, defined before any assignment happens. The **individual treatment effect** is

$$
\tau_i=Y_i(1)-Y_i(0).
$$

Two assumptions are doing silent work, and they are collected under the name SUTVA. **Consistency** links potentials to observation:

$$
Y_i=T_iY_i(1)+(1-T_i)Y_i(0),
$$

which asserts that the treatment is well enough defined that "treated" means the same thing for every unit. **No interference** asserts that unit \(i\)'s outcome does not depend on unit \(j\)'s treatment, which fails in ranking systems, marketplaces, shared caches, and any setting where a model update changes user behavior that other users see.

Because \(\tau_i\) is never observed for any unit, the targets are averages. The three that matter most:

$$
\text{ATE}=E[Y(1)-Y(0)],\qquad
\text{ATT}=E[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid T=1],\qquad
\text{CATE}(x)=E[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X=x].
$$

These are different numbers and different questions. The ATE answers "what if we treated everyone"; the ATT answers "what did treatment do for those who got it"; the CATE answers "what would it do for units like this one." Estimators are not interchangeable across them, and a method that identifies one may not identify another. Deciding which one your decision requires is the first analytic step, not a technicality.

**Worked example — three deployment questions, three estimands.** A safety filter is currently applied to 4% of traffic flagged by a classifier. "Should we keep the filter on the flagged traffic?" is an ATT question. "Should we apply it to all traffic?" is an ATE question, and it requires extrapolating to units the filter has never touched. "Which segments should get it?" is a CATE question. A single analysis that reports one number and answers all three is answering at most one of them.

> **Practice — Foundation:** A unit has \(Y(1)=0.8\), \(Y(0)=0.5\) and is treated. Use consistency to write its observed \(Y\). Then suppose \"treated\" sometimes means the new model at temperature 0.2 (outcome 0.8) and sometimes at temperature 1.0 (outcome 0.6): explain what consistency rules out.
>
> **Hint:** \(Y=TY(1)+(1-T)Y(0)=0.8\); consistency requires one well-defined version of treatment, so two temperatures with different outcomes make \(Y(1)\) ill-defined.
>
> **Practice — Core:** For a 60/40 population split where treatment helps group A by 3 and hurts group B by 1, compute the ATE and the ATT when treatment is given only to group A.
>
> **Hint:** The ATE weights the group effects by population shares, \(0.6(3)+0.4(-1)=1.4\); the ATT weights by the treated units' shares, which here are 100% group A, so it is 3.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** A marketplace has 100 sellers and 1,000 daily sales that a ranking change only redistributes. In an A/B test, the 50 boosted sellers average 18 sales and the 50 others average 2. Compute the naive treated-minus-control difference and the effect of boosting all sellers (everyone back to 10), explain which assumption fails, and state an estimand that remains meaningful.
>
> **Hint:** The naive difference is 16 but the global effect is 0, because control sellers' outcomes depend on others' treatment; a total (global) effect estimated by randomizing whole markets or clusters stays meaningful.

## 2. What randomization buys, and exactly what it does not

Randomized assignment makes \(T\) independent of the potential outcomes:

$$
(Y(1),Y(0))\perp T.
$$

This is why the difference in observed means identifies the ATE:

$$
E[Y\mid T=1]-E[Y\mid T=0]
=E[Y(1)\mid T=1]-E[Y(0)\mid T=0]
=E[Y(1)]-E[Y(0)].
$$

The first equality is consistency; the second is independence. Both steps are visible, and only the second requires randomization.

Note what randomization does *not* supply. It does not supply no-interference, which is a property of the system, not the assignment. It does not survive post-treatment filtering: if you analyze only sessions that completed, and treatment affects completion, the surviving groups are no longer comparable. It does not make small samples balanced — it makes imbalance *random*, which is what the inference in lessons 07 and 08 accounts for. And it does not extend to the population you did not sample from; randomization gives internal validity, sampling design gives external validity, and lesson 10's coverage discussion is the other half of any deployment claim.

Under non-random assignment, the independence above is replaced by a conditional version, **ignorability** or **unconfoundedness**:

$$
(Y(1),Y(0))\perp T\mid X.
$$

Treatment is as-if randomized within cells of \(X\). This is the assumption every adjustment method in the next twelve sections depends on, in one form or another. It is untestable from the observed data, because it constrains the joint distribution of quantities that are never jointly observed.

**Worked example — intention to treat versus the analysis you want.** In a rollout where 30% of assigned users never actually received the new model, comparing *receivers* to *non-receivers* destroys randomization, because receipt is a choice. Comparing by *assignment* preserves it and identifies the intention-to-treat effect, which is a different, smaller, and honestly identified quantity. Section 15 shows how the assignment can then be used as an instrument to recover an effect for compliers.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Four units have \((Y(1),Y(0),T)=(1,0,1),(1,1,1),(0,0,0),(1,0,0)\). List the entries an analyst actually observes, state ignorability, and explain why the observed entries cannot test it.
>
> **Hint:** You see \(Y(1)\) only for units 1 and 2 and \(Y(0)\) only for units 3 and 4; ignorability \((Y(1),Y(0))\perp T\mid X\) constrains quantities that are never observed together for any unit.
>
> **Practice — Core:** Show the two-line derivation that a randomized difference in means equals the ATE, naming the assumption used at each step, and apply it to an A/B test with success rates 0.42 (treatment) and 0.37 (control).
>
> **Hint:** Consistency turns \(E[Y\mid T=t]\) into \(E[Y(t)\mid T=t]\); independence of \(T\) from \(Y(t)\) removes the conditioning, so the ATE estimate is \(0.05\).
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** In a correctly randomized test, 60% of users are \"strong\" and complete the session in both arms with satisfaction 0.9; 40% are \"weak\", never complete under control, and complete with probability 0.5 under treatment with satisfaction 0.5. Treatment changes nobody's satisfaction. Compute the headline metric \"mean satisfaction among completed sessions\" in each arm and locate the failure precisely.
>
> **Hint:** Control completers are all strong (0.9); treatment completers are \(0.6\) strong and \(0.2\) weak of the population, giving \((0.54+0.10)/0.8=0.80\); conditioning on completion, a post-treatment variable, breaks the randomization.

## 3. Identification precedes estimation

An estimand is **identified** when it can be written as a functional of the distribution of observed variables. Identification is a property of assumptions plus the observational regime; it has nothing to do with sample size. If a quantity is not identified, an infinite sample leaves it unknown, and the appearance of a narrow confidence interval means the interval is answering a different question than you think.

The working order is therefore fixed:

1. **Estimand.** Write the causal quantity in potential-outcome notation.
2. **Identification.** Prove it equals a functional of observables, listing every assumption.
3. **Estimation.** Choose an estimator for that functional.
4. **Inference.** Quantify sampling uncertainty in the estimator.
5. **Sensitivity.** Ask how much the answer moves when step 2's assumptions are wrong.

Most applied failures happen at step 2 and are then debated at steps 3 and 4. Switching from ordinary least squares to gradient boosting, or from model-based to cluster-robust standard errors, changes steps 3 and 4 and leaves an identification failure exactly where it was.

**Worked example — the flexible-model temptation.** A team fits a large gradient-boosted model of quality on 400 logged features including a retrieval indicator, then reads the partial dependence of the retrieval feature as its effect. The model is a superb estimator of \(E[Y\mid X]\). It is not an estimator of anything causal unless the 400 features happen to satisfy a backdoor condition, and if a post-treatment feature is among them, flexibility makes the bias *worse* by fitting the mediated path more accurately.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Define identification without referring to sample size, then write the ATE of the section 0 Core scenario as a functional of \(P(D)\) and \(E[Y\mid T,D]\) under ignorability given \(D\) and evaluate it.
>
> **Hint:** The functional is \(\sum_dP(D=d)\bigl(E[Y\mid T=1,d]-E[Y\mid T=0,d]\bigr)=0.5(0.05)+0.5(0.10)=0.075\); it is fixed by the observed distribution, whatever \(n\) is.
>
> **Practice — Core:** Suppose difficulty \(D\) is not logged, so only \(E[Y\mid T=1]=0.67\) and \(E[Y\mid T=0]=0.82\) are available. Construct a second model with no confounding that reproduces these numbers but has ATE \(-0.15\), and name the assumption that identified the ATE of \(0.075\) in the original setting.
>
> **Hint:** Let \(T\) be assigned at random with \(Y(1)\) mean 0.67 and \(Y(0)\) mean 0.82 for everyone; both models give the same observed law, so the ATE needs exchangeability given an observed \(D\) (plus consistency and positivity).
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Let \(D\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\), \(T=\mathbf 1\{D+\eta>0\}\), latency \(L=2T+\nu\), and quality \(Y=0.5L-D+\epsilon\) with independent standard-normal noises. Give the coefficient on \(T\) when regressing \(Y\) on \((T,D)\) and on \((T,D,L)\), say which model predicts \(Y\) better, and explain why the better predictor gives the worse causal answer.
>
> **Hint:** \(E[Y\mid T,D]=T-D\) gives coefficient 1 (the total effect), while \(E[Y\mid T,D,L]=0.5L-D\) gives 0; adding the mediator \(L\) raises \(R^2\) but removes the path through which retrieval acts.

## 4. Causal DAGs make the assumptions writable

A **causal directed acyclic graph** has one node per variable and an arrow \(A\to B\) when \(A\) is a direct cause of \(B\) relative to the variables in the graph. The graph is a compact encoding of a structural model: each variable is a function of its parents and an independent noise term,

$$
V_j=f_j(\mathrm{pa}(V_j),U_j),\qquad U_1,\dots,U_p\text{ jointly independent}.
$$

Missing arrows are the content. An arrow you draw claims only that an effect may exist; an arrow you omit claims that it does not. The omitted-arrow assumptions are the strong ones, and they are the ones the graph forces you to write down rather than leave implicit in a variable list.

Two consequences follow immediately. First, the joint distribution factorizes along the graph,

$$
p(v_1,\dots,v_p)=\prod_{j=1}^p p(v_j\mid \mathrm{pa}(v_j)),
$$

which is the Markov property for DAGs. Second, intervention has a clean graphical meaning: \(\operatorname{do}(T=t)\) deletes every arrow *into* \(T\) and fixes its value, producing the **truncated factorization**

$$
p(v\mid \operatorname{do}(T=t))=\prod_{j:V_j\neq T} p(v_j\mid \mathrm{pa}(v_j))\Big|_{T=t}.
$$

Everything downstream keeps its mechanism; only the assignment mechanism is replaced. This single formula generates the adjustment results of sections 7 and 8.

**Worked example — writing the routing graph.** For the retrieval example: query difficulty \(D\to\) routing \(T\), \(D\to\) quality \(Y\), and \(T\to Y\). Drawing it takes ten seconds and makes the problem obvious: there is a path \(T\leftarrow D\to Y\) that carries association without causation. It also makes the *fix* precise — anything that blocks that path suffices — and exposes the uncomfortable question of whether the logged difficulty score is the real \(D\) or a noisy proxy for it.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Write the Markov factorization for the binary chain \(A\to B\to C\to D\) with \(P(A=1)=0.5\) and, for each arrow, \(P(\text{child}=1\mid\text{parent}=1)=0.8\), \(P(\text{child}=1\mid\text{parent}=0)=0.2\), and compute \(P(A=B=C=D=1)\).
>
> **Hint:** Each node contributes one factor given its parent: \(p(a)p(b\mid a)p(c\mid b)p(d\mid c)=0.5\times0.8^3=0.256\).
>
> **Practice — Core:** Draw the DAG for a logged evaluation where model version \(V\) affects both latency \(L\) and quality \(Q\), and latency affects user retries \(R\). Write its Markov factorization and decide from the graph whether \(Q\perp R\mid V\).
>
> **Hint:** The factorization is \(p(v)p(l\mid v)p(q\mid v)p(r\mid l)\); the only path \(Q\leftarrow V\to L\to R\) is blocked by conditioning on \(V\), so yes.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** On \((T,X,Y)\) compare the complete DAGs \(G_1\): \(X\to T,X\to Y,T\to Y\) and \(G_2\): \(T\to X,X\to Y,T\to Y\). Show neither implies any conditional independence, then, given \(E[Y\mid T,X]=T+2X\) and \(E[X\mid T]=0.5T\) (linear), compute the effect of a unit increase in \(T\) under each graph and relate the result to identification.
>
> **Hint:** Both graphs fit every distribution, so data cannot choose between them; \(G_1\) makes \(X\) a confounder (effect 1) while \(G_2\) makes it a mediator (effect \(1+2(0.5)=2\)): only omitted arrows carry identifying content.

## 5. Chains, forks, and colliders behave differently

Three elementary three-node structures generate every reading rule. Take \(A\), \(B\), \(C\).

**Chain (mediation):** \(A\to B\to C\). Here \(A\) and \(C\) are dependent, and conditioning on \(B\) makes them independent. \(B\) transmits the association; blocking \(B\) stops it. If \(B\) is a mediator of a causal effect you want, conditioning on it removes exactly the part of the effect you were trying to measure.

**Fork (common cause):** \(A\leftarrow B\to C\). Again \(A\) and \(C\) are dependent, and conditioning on \(B\) makes them independent. This is confounding: the dependence is real but not causal, and adjustment removes it.

**Collider (common effect):** \(A\to B\leftarrow C\). Here \(A\) and \(C\) are *independent*, and conditioning on \(B\) — or on any descendant of \(B\) — makes them *dependent*. This is the structure that reverses the usual intuition, and it is the reason "control for more variables" is not a conservative default.

![Chains and forks transmit association until you condition on the middle node; colliders transmit none until you condition, and then they manufacture it.](../assets/causal-paths-collider.svg)

The collider case deserves a concrete mechanism. Suppose \(A\) and \(C\) are independent coin flips and \(B=A+C\). Knowing \(A\) says nothing about \(C\). But knowing \(B=1\) makes them perfectly anti-dependent: \(A=1\) forces \(C=0\). Selection on a common effect creates association between its causes, which is why filtered datasets acquire correlations that the unfiltered population does not have.

**Worked example — why "parses correctly" is dangerous to filter on.** Let model capability \(A\) and prompt formatting quality \(C\) be independent in your corpus, and let both raise the probability that an output parses, \(B\). If you evaluate only on parsed outputs, capability and formatting become negatively correlated inside your evaluation set: among parsed outputs, a weak model must have had good formatting. Any analysis conditioned on that filter inherits the induced dependence, and the induced sign can be opposite to the population sign.

## 6. d-separation reads independences off the graph

A **path** is any sequence of adjacent nodes, ignoring arrow direction. A path is **blocked** by a conditioning set \(S\) when at least one of the following holds:

1. the path contains a chain \(\cdot\to B\to\cdot\) or a fork \(\cdot\leftarrow B\to\cdot\) with \(B\in S\); or
2. the path contains a collider \(\cdot\to B\leftarrow\cdot\) with \(B\notin S\) and no descendant of \(B\) in \(S\).

Sets \(A\) and \(C\) are **d-separated** by \(S\) when every path between them is blocked. The soundness theorem says d-separation implies conditional independence in every distribution compatible with the graph:

$$
A\perp_d C\mid S\ \Longrightarrow\ A\perp C\mid S.
$$

The converse holds for almost all parameterizations — the exceptions are **faithfulness** violations, where two paths cancel exactly. A canonical example: \(T\to M\to Y\) with effect \(+2\) and \(T\to Y\) with effect \(-2\) produces zero total association despite two live causal paths. Faithfulness is an assumption, and exact cancellation is not merely a measure-zero curiosity in engineered systems where a controller is actively tuned to null out an effect.

Notice the asymmetry in rule 2: colliders are blocked *by default* and opened by conditioning, including by conditioning on a descendant. A sample restriction, a dropped row, a filter, or a stratification are all conditioning operations, whether or not they appear in your model formula.

**Worked example — a descendant is enough.** In \(A\to B\leftarrow C\) with \(B\to S\), conditioning on \(S\) partially determines \(B\) and therefore opens the collider. If \(S\) is "the row survived deduplication" and \(B\) is a quality score, deduplicating on quality opens a path between everything that causes quality.

> **Practice — Foundation:** For the collider path \(A\to B\leftarrow C\) with \(B\to S\), and for the fork path \(A\leftarrow B\to C\), say whether the path is blocked given \(\varnothing\) and given \(\{B\}\), and for the collider also given \(\{S\}\). Name the rule used each time and which rule is reversed.
>
> **Hint:** Collider: blocked, open, open (a descendant counts); fork: open, blocked. Rule 1 blocks by conditioning on a noncollider; rule 2 blocks by not conditioning on a collider or its descendants.
>

## 7. Confounding and the backdoor criterion

A **backdoor path** from \(T\) to \(Y\) is a path that begins with an arrow *into* \(T\). Such a path carries association that is not causal, because it flows against the direction of assignment. A set \(S\) satisfies the **backdoor criterion** relative to \((T,Y)\) when

1. \(S\) blocks every backdoor path from \(T\) to \(Y\); and
2. \(S\) contains no descendant of \(T\).

The second clause is not decorative. Conditioning on a descendant of \(T\) either blocks part of the causal effect (if it is a mediator) or opens a collider (if it is a common effect of \(T\) and something else). Both are ways of making the answer worse by adding a variable, and both are invisible to any goodness-of-fit statistic.

When \(S\) satisfies the criterion, the backdoor adjustment formula holds:

$$
P(Y=y\mid \operatorname{do}(T=t))=\sum_{s}P(Y=y\mid T=t,S=s)\,P(S=s),
$$

and in mean form,

$$
E[Y(t)]=E_S\big[E[Y\mid T=t,S]\big].
$$

Read the formula carefully, because the two distributions over \(S\) differ deliberately: the inner expectation conditions on \(S=s\) *and* \(T=t\), while the outer average uses the *marginal* distribution of \(S\). Conditioning uses \(P(S\mid T)\); intervening uses \(P(S)\). That single substitution is the whole of adjustment.

The graphical criterion and the potential-outcome condition are the same assumption in two languages: a set satisfying the backdoor criterion yields \((Y(1),Y(0))\perp T\mid S\).

**Worked example — which variables to adjust for, and which to refuse.** In the routing graph, \(\{D\}\) satisfies the backdoor criterion. Adding response latency — caused by \(T\) — violates clause 2, because latency is a mediator of retrieval's effect; adjusting for it estimates a direct effect that no deployment decision corresponds to. Adding "user complained" — caused by both \(T\) and \(Y\) — is collider conditioning and induces bias where none existed.
